Michelle Bailey Armada Township Planning and Zoning Administrator Publish 9/30/2026 MEMORANDUM TO: Armada Township Planning Commission; Armada Township Board FROM: Macomb County Planning and Economic Development DATE: October 1, 2026 RE: Ord. 114-49 — Proposed Text for Sections 16.41 and 16.42, and a “Year-Round Kitchen” Definition Purpose of This Memorandum Ordinance 114-49 comes before the Planning Commission in September. This memorandum proposes replacement text for two of its sections and the definitions that support them. • Separating the two sections. Section 16.41 (beverage manufacture) and Section 16.42 (year-round kitchens) are written as a coupled pair, so a farm that grows food but makes no alcohol has no path to a kitchen, and a winery seeking only a tasting room must apply under a section about food. Ord. 114-49 begins the separation but does not finish it. The proposed text lets each section stand alone. • Closing definitional gaps. “Year-round kitchen” is used in four places and defined nowhere. So are “operator,” “bona fide farm,” “tasting room,” and “event” — the last of which carries a 300-guest cap in Section 16.39 and day-ofweek limits in Section 16.40. Ten definitions are proposed. • Avoiding conflict with the Right to Farm Act and the GAAMPs. The 2026 Farm Markets GAAMP places on-site processing and restaurants outside Right to Farm protection, which supports regulating both sections, but treats tasting rooms as farm markets and farm-to-table dinners as protected marketing. The proposed text states where Township authority stops rather than inviting a fight over it. • Grounding the intensity standards in local conditions. The occupancy, floor area, and setback limits reflect the capacity of the rural road network serving the AG district, the absence of public water, sewer, and hydrant service, emergency response conditions in the Township, and the Township’s interest in limiting the conversion of productive farmland to parking. They are land use standards and are not intended to limit the volume a licensed manufacturer may produce, which is governed by state law. • Tracking the law developing under Peninsula Township. That litigation produced roughly $50 million in damages against a township whose winery ordinance used geographic sourcing requirements, hours limits, and open-ended terms. The proposed text removes the geographic element from the operator-grown standard, defers to state liquor licensing, and replaces subjective language with measurable standards. Items requiring a Commission decision, questions for the Township Attorney, and conforming amendments needed in other sections are set out in the accompanying memorandum. Proposed Section 16.41 Section 16.41 BEVERAGE PRODUCTION AND TASTING ROOMS A. Applicability and Intent 1. This Special Approval Land Use permits the Applicant to manufacture beverages, including the distillation, fermentation, brewing, and related packaging of alcoholic beverages, and to operate an accessory Tasting Room. 2. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to regulate a farm or farm operation in any manner preempted by the Michigan Right to Farm Act, 1981 PA 93, as amended, or by generally accepted agricultural and management practices developed under that act. Where a Tasting Room independently satisfies the definition of a farm market under those practices, this Section shall not be applied to the marketing activities protected thereunder. This Section continues to apply to beverage production, processing, and storage, and to activities not protected under that act. B. Minimum Site Requirements 1. The site shall be a Bona Fide Farm in active agricultural production, evidenced in the manner provided in Section 8.01(B)(1). 2. Beverage production under this Section may only be considered on a site with a minimum land area of twenty (20) acres or more. 3. The site shall have at least five (5) planted acres of fruit or other crop used in the wine, cider, microbrewery or spirit processing, maintained pursuant to generally accepted agricultural and management practices. 4. At least fifty (50) percent by weight of the fruit and other crops used to make alcoholic beverages on the site shall be grown by the Operator, on the site or on an affiliated farm under the same ownership or control, wherever located. Compliance shall be measured as an average over the three (3) most recent complete calendar years in which the Operator harvested a crop. This requirement may be waived in the case of catastrophic crop failure. 5. The total enclosed floor area of buildings and roofed structures used for beverage processing, storage, sales, and the Tasting Room shall not exceed two percent (2%) of the contiguous lot area, and shall in no case exceed fifty thousand (50,000) square feet. Uncovered outdoor areas shall not be counted toward this limit. 6. The Tasting Room and associated retail sales area shall occupy no more than twenty percent (20%) of the floor area permitted under subsection B.5, or ten thousand (10,000) square feet, whichever is less. C. Setbacks 1. Buildings and structures used for beverage production, processing, storage, sales, or the Tasting Room, together with loading areas, internal truck circulation routes, and any accessory outdoor seating area, shall be located at least one hundred (100) feet from any adjacent property line. 2. Any outdoor crushing or pressing area permitted under subsection F.1 shall be located at least two hundred (200) feet from any adjacent property line. 3. Front and rear yards are as required in the AG district. Where a standard in this subsection is more restrictive, it shall control. D. Tasting Room 1. A Tasting Room is permitted as an accessory use to beverage production approved under this Section. 2. The Tasting Room may be used for the sampling, on-premises consumption, and retail sale of beverages produced on the premises, to the extent authorized by the license held by the Operator or by the entity responsible for such service. 3. Food offered in a Tasting Room shall be limited to pre-packaged items requiring no preparation on the premises. Food service beyond this limit requires approval as a Year-Round Kitchen under Section 16.42, or operation as a Seasonal Kitchen Facility under Section 8.01(B)(2)(i). 4. Maximum occupancy of the Tasting Room, including any accessory outdoor seating area, shall not exceed three hundred (300) persons as determined by the Fire Department. * ALTERNATIVE for Commission consideration — add as D.5: The Planning Commission may approve a maximum occupancy greater than three hundred (300) persons upon a finding that parking, traffic capacity, onsite wastewater capacity, and emergency access are adequate to serve the proposed occupancy. — This would keep 300 as the default while allowing a site that can demonstrate capacity to exceed it, and responds to the objection that a fixed number does not account for demonstrated site capacity. The same provision could be added to Section 16.42 if the Commission wishes. E. Parking. One (1) space for each one hundred (100) square feet of Tasting Room floor area, or one (1) space for each two (2) persons allowed within maximum occupancy as determined by the Fire Department, whichever is greater, plus one (1) space for each employee on the largest work shift. F. Other Requirements 1. All beverage production, processing, bottling, and storage shall be conducted within a completely enclosed building, except that crushing and pressing may be conducted outdoors during the harvest season in an area designated on the approved site plan. 2. All proper permitting and licensing records, as required, shall be available to the Township upon request. 3. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to authorize or prohibit any activity that is authorized or prohibited by the Michigan Liquor Control Code of 1998, as amended, or the rules of the Michigan Liquor Control Commission. G. Traffic Study 1. In order to help ensure safe and reasonable traffic operating conditions on streets and intersections after development of the site, the Township shall require a traffic impact study. 2. A traffic study shall include, at a minimum, a description of existing traffic conditions, forecasted trip generation and forecasted trip distribution, a level of service analysis, the proposed access design for the site, and proposed mitigation measures, if needed. 3. The traffic impact study shall be prepared and submitted by the Applicant, at the Applicant’s sole expense, by a registered Professional Engineer specializing in the preparation of traffic studies. 4. This requirement shall be waived where the maximum occupancy does not exceed one hundred (100) persons, unless the Planning Commission finds that documented sight distance limitations, crash history, or access conditions at the site warrant a study. 5. Access design and traffic control measures shall be subject to the review and approval of the Macomb County Department of Roads. H. Combined Uses. Where beverage production under Section 16.41 and a Year-Round Kitchen under Section 16.42 are both approved on the same site, the combined enclosed floor area of all buildings and roofed structures devoted to those uses shall not exceed the limit in Section 16.41(B)(5), and the combined maximum occupancy of the Tasting Room and the Year-Round Kitchen shall not exceed three hundred (300) persons as determined by the Fire Department. Proposed Section 16.42 Section 16.42 YEAR-ROUND KITCHENS WITH SEATING AREAS A. Applicability and Intent 1. This Special Approval Land Use permits the Applicant to operate a Year-Round Kitchen with a seating area as an accessory use to a Bona Fide Farm. 2. Approval under this Section is not contingent upon the production of beverages on the site. A Year-Round Kitchen may be approved in connection with beverage production approved under Section 16.41, or independently. 3. A Year-Round Kitchen is not a Restaurant. An establishment at which the preparation and service of food is the principal use of the premises is a Restaurant. B. Eligibility and Minimum Site Requirements 1. The site shall be a Bona Fide Farm in active agricultural production, evidenced in the manner provided in Section 8.01(B)(1). 2. A Year-Round Kitchen shall only be permitted on a site twenty (20) acres in size or greater. 3. The total enclosed floor area of buildings and roofed structures used for the Year-Round Kitchen, including seating areas, food preparation, and associated storage, shall not exceed one and one-half percent (1.5%) of the contiguous lot area, and shall in no case exceed four thousand (4,000) square feet. Uncovered outdoor seating areas shall not be counted toward this limit. C. Accessory Character 1. A Year-Round Kitchen shall remain an accessory use to the Bona Fide Farm on the site. Accessory character shall be determined solely by the standard in subsection C.2 and not by any other measure. 2. Gross Receipts attributable to the Year-Round Kitchen, together with Gross Receipts attributable to all other accessory uses approved on the site under Section 8.01(B) and this Article, shall not exceed fifty (50) percent of the total Gross Receipts of the farm operation, measured as an average of gross sales for up to the previous five (5) years, or as outlined in a business plan submitted by the Applicant. 3. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to regulate a farm or farm operation in any manner preempted by the Michigan Right to Farm Act, 1981 PA 93, as amended, or by generally accepted agricultural and management practices developed under that act. Commercial activities not protected by that act remain subject to this Ordinance. 4. The Operator shall certify compliance with subsection C.2 annually to the Zoning Administrator. Records sufficient to substantiate the certification shall be available to the Township upon request in the manner provided in Section 8.01(B)(7)(a). D. Seating and Capacity 1. The area serving food shall seat no more than one hundred fifty (150) patrons at one time, including both indoor and outdoor seating. 2. No more than fifty (50) of the seats permitted under subsection D.1 may be located in an accessory outdoor seating area. E. Events 1. For purposes of this Section, an Event includes both a Private Event and an Event open to the general public, as those terms are defined in Section 20.01. A reservation by a single party that does not close the Year-Round Kitchen to the general public is not an Event. 2. Events are not permitted under this Section and require approval as an Event Hosting Facility under Section 16.39 or as a Special Outdoor Event under Section 16.40. 3. This subsection does not limit farm-to-table dinners, harvest suppers, cooking classes, farm tours, or similar activities that market farm products produced on the affiliated farm. F. Other Requirements 1. Food and beverage service shall be completed at 11:00 p.m. 2. The facility must be licensed to prepare and serve food by the appropriate Health Agency. 3. Alcoholic beverages may be served or sold at retail provided the Operator, or the entity responsible for such service, holds the appropriate license issued by the Michigan Liquor Control Commission. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to authorize or prohibit any activity that is authorized or prohibited by the Michigan Liquor Control Code of 1998, as amended, or the rules of the Michigan Liquor Control Commission. 4. The Applicant shall demonstrate that sanitary and wastewater facilities are adequate to serve the maximum occupancy of the Year-Round Kitchen. G. Setbacks 1. Buildings and structures used for the Year-Round Kitchen shall be located at least one hundred (100) feet from any adjacent property line. 2. Outdoor seating areas shall be located at least one hundred (100) feet from any adjacent property line. 3. Front and rear yards are as required in the AG district. Where a standard in this subsection is more restrictive, it shall control. H. Parking. One (1) space for each one hundred (100) square feet of floor

R2026-02 THE TOWNSHIP BOARD OF THE TOWNSHIP OF ARMADA, MACOMB COUNTY, MICHIGAN, ORDAINS: Section 1. Preamble. Whereas, in order to promote, preserve and protect public health, safety and welfare and to provide for the orderly and proper maintenance of structures, preserve and protect property values, promote harmonious use of land, eliminate blight and preserve and protect neighborhood values and the value and integrity of structures for the purpose of promoting and protecting public health, safety and welfare, Subsection 3 of Section 3 of the Township’s Waste Collection and Disposal Ordinance No. R2026-02 is revised and restated to read as follows: Section 2. Fees for Collection and Disposal Scope of Services Rendered to Single Family Generation Sites. (3) Fees for Collection and Disposal Scope of Services Rendered to Single Family Generation Sites. (A) The owner/occupant of a single family generation site is responsible to pay for the collection and disposal scope of services rendered to the site at the unit prices established by the contract between the Township and Designated Single Waste Hauler. (B) The Designated Single Waste Hauler is responsible for billing and collection of the fees incurred for collection and disposal of services rendered to a single family generation site. (C) The charges for collection and disposal fees relating to services to single-family generation sites by the designated waste hauler shall constitute a lien on the single- family generation site for which the services have been provided. Any charges and penalties delinquent for ninety (90) or more as of September 30" of each year shall be entered upon the following Winter tax roll against the single-family generation site for which the services have been rendered, and the charges and penalties shall be collected as part of the general township taxes against such single-family generation Heme coal LUTE | TTT dL Il Wl site and shall accrue further interest and penalties and shall be collected in the same manner as provided for delinquent real property taxes in the township. The balance placed on a tax roll for collection pursuant to this subsection shall not exceed the cumulative delinquent balance for six months of services to the single family generation site per contract year. Section 3. Repealer. All ordinances or parts of ordinances in conflict herewith are repealed only to the extent necessary to give this ordinance full force and effect. Section 4. Severability. If any article, section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase, or portion of this ordinance is held invalid or unconstitutional by any court of competent jurisdiction, such portion shall be deemed a separate, distinct, and independent provision and such holding shall not affect the validity of remaining portions of the ordinance, it being the intent of the Township that this ordinance shall be fully severable. Will bring buffer map to next meeting to show 500 ft to property line. Woolf and Yurk discussed cooling towers and mechanical screening. Woods asked about noise issues with cooling towers. Lighting, wall packs, glare, foot candles. Percentage of clear doors and windows required. Landscape and buffers. Storm water and wastewater will include Washtenaw County. Professional study required. No well. Needs to be public water. Construction hours discussed. Planner Pezzotti recommended discussing the next sections H, I and J at October meeting. November will discuss sections K and L. 8. Public Comment opened at 8:04 pm. Public comments closed at 8:20 pm. 9. Communications Planner Pezzotti had no more comments. 10. Motion carries unanimously to close the meeting at 8:21 p.m. 2026-9-16 Planning Commission Meeting Minutes Draft *NEW* SECTION 6.26: High Resource Demand Facilities A. Purpose and Intent. The purpose of this ordinance is to establish a regulatory framework for siting, design, operation, and decommissioning of High Resource Demand Facilities, which include Data Centers and Data Processing Centers, in order to balance local economic benefits with protection of public health, safety, welfare, natural resources, and neighborhood character. Standards are intended to: 1. Direct High Resource Demand Facilities to locations with existing and adequate infrastructure, redevelopment and infill of existing sites, and minimal land-use conflicts; 2. Avoid and mitigate nuisance impacts (noise, vibration, light/glare, air emissions); 3. Ensure efficient use of electricity and water, prioritizing renewable energy and conservation; 4. Promote context-appropriate architecture and robust screening; 5. Ensure compatibility with adjacent land uses and the Township’s Master Plan; and 6. Ensure responsible decommissioning and site restoration. B. Applicability. This section applies to High Resource Demand Facilities, Data Center and Data Processing Center uses, including Large-Scale, Small-Scale, and Accessory as defined herein. 1. High Resource Demand Facilities, Data Center and Data Processing Center uses, including Large-Scale, Small-Scale are not permitted as a principal use unless approved as a Planned Unit Development for the purpose of a High Resource Demand Facilities, Data Center and Data Processing Center and adopted through the PUD process set forth in Article 12. 2. Approval is contingent upon the applicant demonstrating conformance to the requirements of this ordinance and other standards of the Zoning Ordinance. 3. Where conflicts exist between this section and other provisions, this section governs. Where silent, other applicable provisions apply (e.g., lighting, landscaping, stormwater, and performance standards). C. Definitions 1. High Resource Demand Facility (HRDF): A principal nonresidential facility, campus, or group of buildings under common ownership or control that is characterized by (i) continuous or near-continuous operation, and (ii) significant mechanical, electrical, or cooling infrastructure, and that meets the applicability criteria in subsections (A) and (B) below. A facility shall be considered an HRDF only when the criteria of both A and B below are met: High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 a) Operational Characteristics. The facility includes one or more of the following operational characteristics that are integral to the primary use: 1. Central plant or large-scale mechanical cooling and/or ventilation systems serving process loads or IT/electronic equipment; 2. On-site emergency generation with an aggregate nameplate capacity exceeding 2,000 kW or 2 MW, and/or on-site fuel storage exceeding 10,000 gallons; 3. Dedicated electrical transformation/switchgear yard, substation, or similarly intensive electrical infrastructure primarily serving the facility; 4. 24-hour operations and/or operational necessity requiring uninterrupted environmental control (temperature/humidity) or high-reliability power systems. b) Resource/Infrastructure Thresholds. The facility exceeds one or more of the following thresholds, as demonstrated by applicant-prepared estimates and utility/service provider documentation, including any phased expansion approved or constructed within five (5) years: 1. Water demand: average daily water demand > 100 gpm; 2. Sanitary sewer: average daily sanitary discharge > 50,000 gallons/day; 3. Electric demand: maximum contracted demand or designed peak demand > 10 MW (or equivalent documented kW); 4. Hazardous materials / regulated wastes: storage, use, or generation requiring reporting under [EPCRA Tier II and/or applicable state hazardous materials reporting] and/or generation of hazardous waste at a level regulated under [state/federal hazardous waste generator requirements], as documented on a materials inventory submitted with the application. Exclusions. HRDF does not include general warehousing/distribution, general manufacturing, office uses, or any other specific use listed in this ordinance unless the Zoning Administrator determines, based on operational characteristics and supporting documentation, that the facility is substantially similar in operational profile to HRDF-type facilities (e.g., high-reliability power demand and continuous environmental control serving electronic/process loads) and meets subsections (A) and (B). Aggregation. Multiple buildings, modules, or phases located on the same site or on contiguous parcels under common ownership or control shall be aggregated for purposes of determining HRDF status and whether thresholds are exceeded. Relationship to Data Centers. A Data Center or Data Processing Center that meets the HRDF definition shall be considered an HRDF and shall comply with all applicable HRDF supplemental standards. 2. Data Center: A facility used for the centralized storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital information, typically containing computer servers, data storage systems, telecommunications equipment, power distribution systems, cooling and 2 High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. ventilation systems, uninterruptible power supplies, backup generators, and associated support infrastructure. The term includes colocation centers, cloud-computing facilities, hyperscale computing facilities, and similar high-intensity information technology operations. The term does not include small server rooms, IT closets, or similar equipment rooms that are clearly accessory and subordinate to another lawful principal use. Data Processing Center: A building or portion of a building used primarily for the manipulation, analysis, computation, or transformation of digital information through computer hardware or specialized equipment. A Data Processing Center may include servers or digital processing equipment, but is typically of smaller scale or lower intensity than a Data Center and may involve office or administrative functions associated with data manipulation. The term does not include general business offices or accessory server rooms subordinate to a principal use. Large-Scale Data Center and Data Processing Center: A center equal or greater than 25,000 sq ft gross floor area or located on a site greater than 10 acres. Small-Scale Data Center and Data Processing Center: A center less than 25,000 sq ft, often serving local or regional networks. Accessory Data Center and Data Processing Center: A center that is clearly incidental and subordinate to a principal use (e.g., hospital, university, large employer) and less than 10,000 sq ft. Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). One or more electrochemical energy storage containers, inverters, switchgear, and associated equipment, which may be co-located with a High Resource Demand Facility to provide resiliency or load management. On-site Substation/Switchyard. Electric utility facilities (e.g., transformers, breakers) necessary to serve a data center. D. Districts Permitted and Process. A HRDF/Data Center/Data Processing Center project, in accordance with Article 12, may only be considered in following zoning districts. 1. Districts a) High Resource Demand Facility: allowed in GI, General Industrial only. Prohibited elsewhere. b) Large-Scale Data Centers and Data Processing Centers: allowed in GI, General Industrial District only. Prohibited elsewhere. c) Small-Scale Data Centers and Data Processing Centers: allowed in GI, General Industrial District and LI, Limited Industrial District. Prohibited elsewhere. d) Accessory Data Centers and Data Processing Centers: allowed as a Special Land Use accessory to a permitted or approved use in the GI, General Industrial, LI, Limited Industrial, GC, General Commercial, and O, Office Districts. Prohibited elsewhere. 2. Process a) For items a-c above, the procedures of Article 12 shall be followed. b) Accessory Data Centers and Data Processing Centers (item d above) shall follow the special land use procedures outlined in Article 4. 3 High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 E. Required Engagement Steps (minimum standards) 1. Pre-application conference (mandatory) a) Applicants shall meet with Township and planning staff prior to submitting an application. b) Staff shall identify expected engagement topics, impacted stakeholders, and the required contents of the Community Engagement Plan. 2. Community Engagement Plan (CEP) (required with application) a) A CEP shall be submitted as part of the application package and must include: o Project overview (site, size, phasing, anticipated construction timeline); o Draft public information materials (fact sheet, FAQs); o Engagement schedule and methods; o Proposed meeting formats and locations (including virtual option); o List/map of stakeholders and the Engagement Area; o Languages and accessibility accommodations; o Communication channels (project website, email list, hotline); o Process for documenting comments and responses; and o Proposed Risk Mitigation b) The Zoning Administrator shall determine whether the CEP is complete prior to scheduling public hearings. 3. Neighborhood meeting(s) (mandatory, prior to first public hearing) a) The applicant shall hold at least one neighborhood meeting no fewer than 21 days and no more than 60 days prior to the first public hearing. b) Notice shall be given to all property owners and addresses (if different) within 500 feet of the proposed project site. If a property is within 500 feet and is part of a subdivision, homeowners, or business owners association, all members of the association shall be notified. c) Additional neighborhood meetings may be required if: o There are significant amendments, based upon determination of the Zoning Administrator, to the plan between Planning Commission or Township Board reviews; or o The Planning Commission or Township Board directs additional engagement due to public interest. d) Meeting requirements: o Held at a location within Augusta Township that is ADA-accessible, and available after 5:00 p.m. on a weekday or on a weekend; o Virtual participation option must be provided; o Applicants must provide interpreters upon request with at least 7 days notice; and o Meeting must include a Q&A segment and accept written comments. 4. Report a) After each neighborhood meeting, the applicant shall submit a report to the Township providing at a minimum, the following meeting details: 4 High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 1. Meeting details (location, time, etc) 2. Meeting sign in sheet 3. Meeting minutes F. Dimensional Standards 1. Minimum Lot Area: a) High Resource Demand Facility: 10 acres b) Large-Scale Data Center and Data Processing Center: 10 acres c) Small-Scale and Accessory Data Center and Data Processing Center: 2 acres. 2. Maximum Building Height: 45 feet / 3 stories 3. Maximum Lot Coverage: 60%. 4. Minimum Setbacks: a) High Resource Demand Facility: 400 feet from any residentially used or zoned property, primary/secondary school, medical clinic, park, day-care center and preschool, hospital or medical center. 200 feet from all other property lines. b) Large-Scale: 400 feet from any residentially used or zoned property, primary/secondary school, medical clinic, park, day-care center and preschool, hospital or medical center. 200 feet from all property lines. c) Small-Scale and Accessory: 100 feet from any residentially used or zoned property, primary/secondary school, medical clinic, park, day-care center and preschool, hospital or medical center. 75 feet from all property lines. 5. Greenbelt: a) A minimum 50-foot landscaped greenbelt shall be provided along all property lines. The greenbelt shall include an opaque screen meeting the Landscaping and Screening requirements of section 5.7. 6. Siting: a) A High Resource Demand Facility, including but not limited to a Large Scale Data Center, shall not be located on any parcel that is within 500 feet of any residential zoned or used property, primary/secondary school, medical clinic, park, day-care center and preschool, hospital or medical center. G. Site and Design Standards 1. Architecture & Façade Articulation a) Massing and Scale 1. Building massing, height, bulk, scale, and proportion shall maintain consistency with the existing character of the adjacent buildings. 2. Building design should employ coordinated massing to produce overall unity, scale, and interest. 3. Rooflines and pitches shall be proportionate to nearby structures so as to provide transition or mitigation of significant changes to scale. b) Architectural design and building materials. 5 High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 c) 1. Facade variation. Wall designs must provide a minimum of three of the following elements, in addition to transparency requirements, occurring at intervals no greater than 25 feet horizontally and 10 feet vertically: a. Expression of structural system and infill panels through change in plane not less than three inches. b. System of horizontal and vertical scaling elements, such as: belt course, string courses, cornice, pilasters. c. System of horizontal and vertical reveals not less than one inch in width/depth. d. Variations in material module, pattern, and/or color. e. System of integrated architectural ornamentation. f. Green screen or planter walls. g. Translucent, fritted, patterned, or colored glazing. h. Transparency as required in Section 6.26(G)(4). 2. Architectural style shall not be restricted. Rather, evaluation of the appearance of a project shall be based upon compatibility and the quality of its design and relationship to surroundings. 3. Buildings within the same development should be designed to provide a unified and easily identifiable image. Methods to achieve this include using similar architectural styles and materials, complementary roof forms, signs, and colors. 4. Minimize monotony of expansive exterior walls by incorporating the following elements: staggering of vertical walls; recessing openings; providing upper-level roof overhangs; using deep score lines at construction joints; contrasting compatible building materials; use of variety and rhythm of window and door openings; use of horizontal and vertical architectural elements, use of horizontal bands of compatible colors; and providing changes in roof shape or roofline. 5. Facades shall provide visual interest from both vehicular and pedestrian viewpoints. 6. Entrances to individual buildings shall be readily identifiable to visitors through the use of recesses or pop-outs, roof elements, columns, or other architectural elements. Material standards. 1. Durable building materials, simple configurations, and solid craftsmanship are required. At least 75% of walls visible from public streets, exclusive of wall areas devoted to meeting transparency requirements, shall be constructed of brick, glass, metal (beams, lintels, trim elements, and ornamentation only), wood lap, stucco, split-faced block, or stone. Vinyl or aluminum siding shall only be used for accents. Exterior Insulation Finishing Systems (E.I.F.S.) or similar material is not permitted as a primary building material. 2. Materials shall be selected for suitability to the type of buildings and the architectural design in which they are used. 6 High Demand Facilities/Data Center Zoning Ordinance Language July 2026 3. Material selection shall be consistent with architectural style in terms of color, shades, and texture; however, monotony shall be avoided. 4. Materials shall be consistent with adjoining buildings. 5. Buildings shall have the same materials, or those that are architecturally compatible, for construction of all building walls and other exterior building components wholly or partly visible from public ways and public parking lots. 6. In any design in which the structural frame is exposed to view, the structural materials shall be compatible within themselves and harmonious with their surroundings. 7. Transitional features. a. Transitional features are architectural elements, site features, or alterations to building massing that are used to provide a transition between higher-intensity uses and low- or moderate-density residential areas. These features assist in mitigating potential conflicts between those uses. Transitional features are intended to be used in combination with landscape buffers or large setbacks. b. Intensity. A continuum of use intensity, where moderate-intensity uses are sited between high-intensity uses and low-intensity uses, shall be developed for multibuilding developments. An example would be an office use between commercial and residential uses. c. Height and mass. Building height and mass in the form of building stepbacks, recess lines or other techniques shall be graduated so that structures with higher-intensity uses are comparable in scale with adjacent structures of lower-intensity uses. … or site orientations to local fire, police, and emergency medical services. 4. Battery Energy Storage Systems (if provided) a) Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) shall be permitted as an accessory component to the principal use of the … shall be permitted as an accessory component to the principal use of the property. b) BESS shall comply with NFPA 855, the Michigan Building/Fire Codes, and manufacturer's specifications. c) Setbacks. Outdoor BESS containers shall be set … e) Applicant shall include a BESS-specific emergency response plan and data sheet package. 5. On-Site Substation/Switchyard (if provided) a) Shall be located to minimize visual and noise impacts; and shall provide evergreen screening and … may retain qualified consultants to review energy efficiency, water use, air quality, BESS safety, renewable energy, stormwater, and related matters. 2. All reasonable costs for these reviews shall be escrowed by the applicant. J.

ULDRIKS DRIVE BATTLE CREEK, MICHIGAN PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES September 22nd, 2026 Call to Order: by Chairman, Mike Staib at 6:00 pm Pledge of Allegiance administered by attending body Roll Call: Chairman Staib, Trustee Gene McKay, Commissioners: Toni Ardis, Kevin Villadsen, Barb Jones, Claudia Brown, Shirley Tuggle. 6 Members Present. Quorum Established. Absence Report: Shirley Tuggle - Absent Approval of September 22nd, 2026, Meeting Agenda: Commissioners received the meeting agenda in their packets. No other additions or deletions were suggested. It was moved by Commissioner Jones and Second by Trustee McKay to approve the meeting agenda. Roll Call 6 in favor/0 opposed. Motion Carries. Approval of August 12th, 2026, Meeting Minutes: Commissioners received a draft copy of the August 12th, 2026, Planning Commission Meeting Minutes. No other additions or deletions were suggested. It was moved by Commissioner Villadsen and Second by Commissionioner Brown to approve the meeting minutes as presented. Roll Call 6 in favor/0 opposed. Motion Carries. Building and Zoning Report: Zoning Administrator, Cody McCarty – Chairman Staib shared that a new format for the Building and Zoning Report is in the process of being designed. It will allow for the streamlining of information and alleviate the need for additional time during the meetings. The report will be sent out in the packets for review each month. Cody shared that the Township Board has received an acceptable design from the design ﬁrm for the new Fire Station and that the site plan will head to the Planning Commission in the next couple of months. Casey’s Gas Station – Applicant has started clearing land. EGLE required a silt fence to be installed and the applicant has complied. Gas Station 3312 (Old Logan’s) - Applicant needs an actual “Boundary Survey” before anything can be reviewed. The Septic System will be designed by the Calhoun County Health Department. MDOT permits are pending. First review from Planners indicate other items need to be addressed as well. Liaison Report: Trustee Gene McKay shared that the Township Board passed the resolution necessary for the moratorium to be sent back to the Planning Commission to proceed with proper draft language. The ﬁrst budget meeting is scheduled for Monday, September 28th, 2026 @ 5:30 pm. The Township Board is in the process of collecting draft budget requests from all departments. Public Comment Time on Agenda Items Only: Open @ 6:11pm Close @ 6:11pm – With No Comments Discussion of Old Business: Boat Launch Custer Drive – Calhoun County has reached out and would like to make a presentation on the Boat Launch Project to the Planning Commission at the October 27th meeting. Presentation documents will be available for Planning Commission members and any attendees. The tentative plan is to have group discussion at the Planning Commission level and send a recommendation over to the Township Board for the November 10th, 2026 Board Meeting. Liaison, Trustee McKay to pass on an invite to the Township Board members to attend the presentation if they so choose to do so. Final Review of Moratorium Proposed Draft Language: The Township Board has o icially, by Resolution given authorization to the Planning Commission to investigate adding moratoriums into the text amendments. McKenna is waiting on draft language from Legal Counsel. The Planning Commission agrees that we authorize the proposed draft language for the use of a temporary general moratorium and a speciﬁc use moratorium regarding Data Centers. We will need to add these under Article 5, General Provisions and titled 5.11 Moratoriums with subtypes Temporary Use and Speciﬁc Use to the Zoning Ordinance. All members agreed that this will be part of the draft language that is proposed for our text amendments. Final Review of Proposed Draft Language for Text Amendments with McKenna The items discussed are from the draft language in the Commissioners packets. Some items are complete and some items need clariﬁcation. Prior to the next meeting you will receive a complete set of track changes from the Planners. 4.17 A 2 – Standards: Remove the no additional standards and add language for Minimum Principal Dwelling Unit shall be 800 square feet for livable ground ﬂoor level living space. Page 26 4.10 - Carry over standards from Boarding/Breeding Kennel to Rescue/Foster/Personal. Additionally create a new use for Rescue/Foster/Personal in the Zoning Ordinance to match the table on Page 9 as it is listed in the Table of Permitted Uses but not in the Zoning Ordinance. Also add Special Land Use under the Mixed-Use District. Add language to both Uses to strengthen Waste Management Plan. Page 22 4.26 5 A I – Insert language deﬁning and referencing Michigan Department of Education (MDE) School Accreditation. Pages 34 36 38 4.27 5 A I – Insert language deﬁning and referencing Michigan Department of Education (MDE) School Accreditation. Pages 41 43 45 47 48 4.28 B - Standards – No Change Page 50 4.33 t – Insurance Page 56 – Consistent Clause under Special Land Use – Add requirement to provide Proof of Insurance under 13.03 Site Plan Review. The Planning Commission could also attach as a reasonable condition of an approval. Page 156 Article 1 – Title, Purpose and Scope – Change Bedford Charter Township to Charter Township of Bedford throughout Zoning Ordinance. Headers on all pages are under a picture format graphic and will need to be addressed by the graphics team at McKenna. All other corrections are made. 2.01 Creation of Districts – No Change - The wording on Master Plan does not need to mirror the Zoning Ordinance. Page 6 4.43 B 2 – Sexually Oriented Business - Add language deﬁning and referencing Michigan Department of Education (MDE) School Accreditation. Page 64 Articles 11 through 13 – Highlight text changes to show up from the 8/12/2026 meeting minutes sent over to Planner. Pages 145-156 highlight 16.01 Deﬁnitions – Planners to create childcare friendly terminology from the State of Michigan for current use. Page 190 16.01 Deﬁnitions – Licensee - Add the wording “Recreational Use” at end of sentence. Page 195 3.02 & 3.03 – Existing Lots – No Change, Need a better understanding of the meaning per McKenna. Legal non-conforming is the language used. No longer using “Grandfather Clause Language”. Page 12 5.07 – Street, Roads and other Means of Access – No Change Page 115 Data Storage Ordinance Moratorium – Being created under ARTICLE 5.11 – Will add draft language as discussed. Page 117 Article 13 – Complete 8-12-26 meeting Pages 156 – 179 Article 14 – Complete 8-12-26 meeting Pages 180 – 184 4.37 – Range- Gun – Indoor – Develop Indoor Gun Range Standards – Complete 8-12-26 meeting 59 Page 4.33 t - Insurance – Previously addressed above. 11.03 A – Procedures for Determining Compliance – O icial Investigation - Change the word “Evidence to Complaint”. – Complete. Page148 12.01 Intent – Are subdivisions considered a PUD? Currently yes. No Change. Page 149 Article 3 - Table of Permitted Uses – Uses under Article 4, draft language from Planners on several items, One incorrect spelling -Complete Page 8 – 12 Article 7 – O -Street Parking Requirements – Schedule chart does not match Article 4 – Proposing to allow market to dictate how much parking is needed. 7.01 C 2 - Barrier Free parking requirements are outdated compared to the state site - Match Article 7 to Article 4 for number of spaces required. Pages 124 - 131 Final review of any additionally proposed draft language for Text Amendments: Nothing Additional from Commission Members Public Comment time: Open @ 8:39pm Close @ 8:39pm - With no comments Planning Commission Member Time: Trustee McKay – Shared Great Job. Chairman Staib- Thanked everyone including Kyle and his sta at McKenna. The goal here is to set the Public Hearing for October. McKenna will get all required documents back to the Planning Commission as soon as possible to try and help facilitate that goal. Kyle – McKenna – Provided vital information regarding newspapers are now starting to go completely electronic with no newspaper to post Hearings in. Many legal entities are working with the state for direction and recommendations. Commission Jones – Inquired about putting Bedford’s history in the Zoning Ordinance book. The group consensus was to incorporate that when we revisit the Master Plan, after checking accuracy of the information. Barb also inquired about adding the members’ names to the Zoning Ordinance book title page under “prepared by”. After some group discussion, it was agreed upon not to move forward with that. The hearing will commence at 6:00 p.m., or as soon thereafter as the matter can be heard, and will be held at the Blackman Charter Township Meeting Hall, 1990 West Parnall Road, Jackson, Michigan. The Series 2026 Bonds are expected to be issued pursuant to New Hampshire RSA 162-S, as amended, and the proceeds from the sale of the Series 2026 Bonds will be loaned to Otterbein Homes, an Ohio nonprofit corporation, its subsidiaries of which it is the sole member and other affiliated entities (collectively, “Otterbein”) and used to (i) retire all or a portion of the outstanding Master Term Note dated March 30, 2026 issued by Otterbein to TD Bank, N.A., (the “Series 2026A Master Note’) originally issued to refund those certain Public Finance Authority $23,830,000 Current Interest and Capital Appreciation Bonds (Vista Grande Villa Project), Series 2022A and Public Finance Authority, $6,745,000 Taxable Convertible Capital Appreciation Revenue Bonds (Vista Grande Villa Project), Series 2022B, in connection with the acquisition by Otterbein Homes of the membership interest in Vista Grande Villa, a Michigan nonprofit corporation and owner of the continuing care retirement community known as “Vista Grande Villa” (the “Facility”) located at 2251 Springport Road, Charter Township of Blackman, County of Jackson, State of Michigan; (ii) establishing one or more debt service reserve funds as additional security for the Series 2026 Bonds, if deemed necessary or desirable by Otterbein; (iii) paying capitalized interest on the Series 2026 Bonds, if any; and (iv) paying certain costs of issuance of the Series 2026 Bonds (collectively, the “Project”). The initial legal owner or principal user of the Project financed or refinanced by the Series 2026 Bonds shall be Vista Grande Villa or a subsidiary or affiliate of Otterbein that is controlled by Otterbein. The Series 2026 Bonds are expected to be issued by the New Hampshire Business Finance Authority of the State of New Hampshire, operating under the name “National Finance Authority” (the “Issuer’’) pursuant to Chapter 331, RSA 162-S, as amended. The Series 2026 Bonds will be special obligations of the Issuer and will not constitute a debt or pledge of the faith and credit or the taxing power of the Issuer. The hearing will provide a reasonable opportunity to be heard for persons wishing to express their views on the merits of the Project, the Facility, the Facility location, the issuance of the Series 2026 Bonds or related matters. The Township Board will consider the approval of the proposed Bond issue only after the public hearing has been completed. Dated: October 5, 2026 MEMORANDUM TO: Township Board of the Charter Township of Blackman Cc: Pete Jancek, Township Supervisor FROM: Craig W. Hammond, Eric McGlothlin, Dickinson Wright PLLC DATE: September 23, 2026 RE: Approval of Host Jurisdiction for Tax-Exempt Bonds Issued by the National Finance Authority for Vista Grande Villa d/b/a Otterbein Jackson Vista Grande Villa d/b/a Otterbein Jackson (“VGV”) is a Michigan nonprofit 501(c)(3) corporation engaged in owning and operating a continuing care retirement community (the “Community”) located at 2251 Springport Road, Blackman Charter Township, Jackson County, Michigan. The parent entity of VGV is Otterbein Homes, an Ohio nonprofit corporation (“Otterbein”). Otterbein desires to refinance certain outstanding indebtedness relating to the Community through the use of tax-exempt “qualified 501(c)(3) bonds”. Otterbein has requested that the National Finance Authority ("NFA") issue the tax-exempt bonds for this transaction. NFA is an issuer with multi-state issuing jurisdiction organized under New Hampshire law. The plan is for NFA to issue its Healthcare Facilities Refunding Revenue Bonds (Otterbein Homes Obligated Group), Series 2026 in one or more series (the “Bonds”), in an amount not to exceed $43,150,000 to refinance certain outstanding indebtedness previously incurred by VGV or Otterbein to finance costs relating to the Community. Under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the "Code"), the Bonds must meet certain requirements in order for the interest on the Bonds to be tax-exempt. Section 147(f)(2)(A) of the Code requires that the issuance of the Bonds must be approved by NFA and each governmental unit having jurisdiction over the area in which any facility is located. The approval requirement is met if the Bonds are approved by, in this case, the elected legislative body of such governmental unit after a public hearing following reasonable public notice. The purpose of the public notice and hearing is to give the local officials and residents an opportunity to provide input, support or raise objections to the Bonds and the proposed uses of the Bond proceeds. With respect to the proposed issuance of the Bonds, the Blackman Charter Township Board (the "Board") is the elected legislative body that must approve the issuance of the Bonds after the public hearing is held. Approval of the Bonds would allow the financing to proceed. Approval of the Bonds would not obligate Blackman Charter Township (the “Township”) to pay any portion of the debt service on the Bonds or in any way pledge the Township’s credit as security for the Bonds or otherwise cause the Township to incur any liability relating to the financing. The Bonds would solely be an obligation of NFA payable from loan payments to be made by Otterbein and certain subsidiaries, including VGV, and any other security provided by Otterbein. It is customary for the public hearing described in this memo to be held at a regularly scheduled meeting, with an approving resolution being adopted thereafter. Federal tax law requires that notice of the Public Hearing must be published at least seven (7) days in advance of the hearing date in either (i) a newspaper of general circulation in the Township or (ii) by electronic posting on the Township’s primary public website in an area of the website used to inform its residents about events affecting the residents, such as notice of public meetings of the Township. VGV is requesting that the Board hold a public hearing at its October 19, 2026 meeting and, upon completion of the public hearing to the Board's satisfaction, adopt a resolution approving issuance of the Bonds. In order to meet the requirements of the Code, we will need to arrange publication or posting of the notice of public hearing at least one week in advance of the public hearing date. When we have confirmed the meeting date, Dickinson Wright PLLC will arrange for publication of the required notice of hearing if posting to the Township website is not an available option. Accompanying this memo are drafts of the public hearing notice and a resolution approving the issuance of the Bonds by NFA. Please let us know if you have any questions or need any further information. We appreciate your assistance in this matter. 4902-4265-9280 v2 [121987-1]

This agenda is posted in compliance with PA 267 of 1976 as amended (Open meetings Act), MCLA 41.72a (2) (3) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The Bridgeport Charter Township Planning Commission will provide necessary reasonable auxiliary aids and services, such as signers for the hearing impaired and audio tapes of printed materials being considered at this meeting, to individuals with disabilities at the meeting or public hearing upon EIGHT (8) day notice to the Township Clerk at (989)-777-0940 ext. 240. 1 Rules of Public Comment & Participation – Planning Commission Meetings The Bridgeport Charter Township Planning Commission recognizes the value of public comments on Township issues and the importance of allowing members of the public to express themselves on matters of community interest. But, for the benefit of all, and in the interest of all, the following rules of participation and public comment shall apply at all meetings as allowed by the Open Meetings Act. The intent of these rules is: 1. To allow members of the public a fair and adequate opportunity to be heard; 2. To grant the Zoning Administrator and/or the presiding member of the Planning Commission the authority to deny any request that an item be placed on the agenda. Such denial shall be based on a determination by the Zoning Administrator and/or presiding member of the Planning Commission that the request is frivolous, harassing or repetitive. 3. To provide adequate time for the Planning Commission to obtain necessary information, conduct fact finding and give thorough consideration to situations in which an individual, during the requested presentation, addresses or questions a Township policy, procedure or decision that does not exist, a change to a Township policy, procedure or decision is proposed, or an exception to a Township policy, procedure or decision is specifically requested by the individual; 4. To assure that the regular agenda of the Planning Commission is completed; and 5. To recognize the nature of the Planning Commissions’ time and to use that time efficiently. Person or Delegations wishing to be placed on the Agenda: An individual or delegation desiring to appear before the Planning Commission may request placement on the agenda by making such request in writing to the Zoning Administrator and/or presiding member of the Planning Commission no less than seven (7) business days before the meeting at which the individual would like to speak. The request shall include, at a minimum, the following information: a. Name of the person or the delegation affiliation, whichever is applicable. b. A detailed summary of the topic to be presented or discussed. The individual making the request will be notified by the Building Administrator and/or presiding member of the Planning Commission as to whether the request has been granted and, if the request is granted, will be provided three (3) minutes to speak, when the individual’s requested topic is addressed on the agenda, unless extended by the presiding officer. The Zoning Administrator and/or presiding member of the Planning Commission shall take appropriate steps to determine that requests that an item be placed on the agenda are not frivolous, repetitive, or harassing in nature. Delegations must select only one individual to speak on their behalf. Individuals speaking to the Planning Commission shall address remarks only to the presiding member of the Township Planning Commission. The presiding member of the Planning Commission shall have the authority to terminate the presentation of any individual who does not adhere to the above rules or is abusive toward an individual Planning Commission member or the Planning Commission as a whole. The presiding member of the Planning Commission, members of the Planning Commission, and the Zoning Administrator may ask questions of any individual addressing the Planning Commission. Public comment: 1. Each presentation to the Planning Commission made by an individual shall be limited to three (3) minutes in duration, unless extended by agreement of the presiding member of the Planning Commission. 2. No individual may speak more than once on the same topic. 3. To ensure that all interested parties have an opportunity to speak, please be brief and limit any comments to one topic. 4. Public comment is not a question and answer period. It provides individuals with an opportunity to express their comments regarding any subject matter. All comments shall be directed only to the presiding member of the Planning Commission; no person may address or question Planning Commission members individually. 5. The Planning Commission will not respond to comments made during the public comment period unless it becomes necessary to ask a clarifying question, correct a factual error, or provide specific factual information. CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF BRIGHTON ZONING ORDINANCE ARTICLE 7 INDUSTRIAL DISTRICT Sec. 7-01 Description and Purpose (a) I-1 Industrial District. The I-1 Industrial District is intended to primarily accommodate wholesale activities, warehouses, and industrial operations whose external, physical effects are restricted to the area of the district and do not have a detrimental effect on any of the surrounding districts and uses. The I-1 District is structured to permit, along with any specified uses, the manufacturing, compounding, processing, packaging, assembly, and/or treatment of finished or semi-finished products from previously prepared material. It is further intended that the processing of raw material for shipment in bulk form, to be used in an industrial operation at another location, not be permitted in locations where surrounding land uses could be adversely affected. The general goals of this district include, among others, the following specific purposes: (1) To provide sufficient space, in appropriate locations, to meet the needs of the Township's expected future economy for a variety of manufacturing and related uses. (2) To protect abutting Residential Districts by separating them from manufacturing activities, and by prohibiting the use of industrial areas for new residential development. (3) To promote manufacturing development which is free from danger of fire, explosions, toxic and noxious matter, radiation, and other hazards, and from offensive noise, vibration, smoke, odor, and other objectionable influences. (4) To promote the most desirable use of land in accordance with a well considered plan. To protect the character and established pattern of adjacent development, and in each area to conserve the value of land and buildings and other structures, and to enhance the Township's tax revenue. Motion Approved Respectfully Submitted: Approved: Kayla Poissant, PC Secretary Lucas Curd, PC Chair High Resource Demand Facility Draft 9.22.26 CONWAY TOWNSHIP ORDINANCE NO. ___ AN ORDINANCE TO REGULATE HIGH RESOURCE DEMAND FACILITIES The Township of Conway ordains: Section 1. New Section 6.28 of the Zoning Ordinance. A new Section 6.28 entitled “High Resource Demand Facilities” is hereby added to the Township’s Zoning Ordinance, to read, in its entirety, as follows: SECTION 6.28: High Resource Demand Facilities A. Purpose and Intent The purpose of this ordinance is to establish a regulatory framework for siting, design, operation, and decommissioning of High Resource Demand Facilities, which include data centers and data processing centers, and similar facilities, to balance local economic benefits with protection of public health, safety, welfare, natural resources, and neighborhood character. Standards are intended to: 1. Direct High Resource Demand Facilities to locations with existing and adequate infrastructure, redevelopment and infill of existing sites, and minimal land-use conflicts; 2. Avoid and mitigate nuisance impacts including noise, vibration, light/glare, and air emissions for neighboring businesses and residences; 3. Ensure efficient use of electricity and water, prioritizing renewable energy and conservation; 4. Promote context-appropriate architecture and robust screening to be compatible with the Township’s rural character and natural resources; 5. Ensure compatibility with adjacent land uses and the Township’s Master Plan, including preservation of agricultural heritage, protection of natural resources, management of traffic, thoughtful planning for future development, and creating a sustainable community; and 6. Ensure responsible decommissioning and site restoration. B. Applicability 1. This section applies to High Resources Demand Facilities, Data Center and Data Processing Center uses, including Large-Scale, Small-Scale, and Accessory as defined herein. 1 High Resource Demand Facility Draft 9.22.26 2. Approval is contingent upon the applicant demonstrating conformance to the requirements of this ordinance and other standards of the Zoning Ordinance. 3. Where conflicts exist between this section and other provisions, this section governs. Where silent, other applicable provisions apply (e.g., lighting, landscaping, stormwater, and performance standards). 4. Required Application Materials. A. In addition to all application materials otherwise required by this Ordinance for Special Land Use and Site Plan review, an application for a High Resource Demand Facility, Data Center, Data Processing Center, or similar high demand facility uses are subject to this Section shall include the following: 1. Risk Mitigation Plan. 2. Community Engagement Plan. 3. Hydrogeological Study. 4. Traffic Management Plan for construction. 5. Hazardous Materials Management Plan. 6. Fire Protection Plan. 7. Emergency Response Plan. 8. Decommissioning and Site Restoration Plan. 9. Development Agreement with the Township. B. The following shall be submitted prior to occupancy and reported on annually: 1. Actual annual energy consumption (MWh) and calculated PUE; 2. Renewable energy procurement and percentage of total load; 3. Water usage (gallons) and cooling method; 4. Waste and heat recovery feasibility analysis; 5. Disposal of hazardous materials and what they were; 6. Long term ground water monitoring; 7. Generator testing/operating hours and emissions compliance statement with current EGLE permits; 8. Sound level monitoring summary; and 2 High Resource Demand Facility Draft 9.22.26 9. High Resource Demand Facility (HRDF): A principal nonresidential facility, campus, or group of buildings under common ownership or control that is characterized by (i) continuous or near-continuous operation, and (ii) significant mechanical, electrical, or cooling infrastructure, and that meets the applicability criteria in subsections (A) and (B) below. A facility shall be considered an HRDF only when sub-section A and sub-section B below are met: A. Operational Characteristics. The facility includes one or more of the following operational characteristics that are integral to the primary use: 1. Central plant or large-scale mechanical cooling and/or ventilation systems 3 High Resource Demand Facility Draft 9.22.26 serving process loads or Information Technology (IT)/electronic equipment; 2. On-site emergency generation with an aggregate nameplate capacity exceeding 2,000 kilowatt (kW), and/or on-site fuel storage exceeding 10,000 gallons; 3. Dedicated electrical transformation/switchgear yard, substation, or similarly intensive electrical infrastructure primarily serving the facility; 4. On-site energy storage facilities that absorbs, stores, and discharges electricity with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more and an energy discharge capacity of 200 megawatt hours or more. 5. 24-hour operations and/or operational necessity requiring uninterrupted environmental control (temperature/humidity) or high-reliability power systems. B. Resource/Infrastructure Thresholds. The facility exceeds one or more of the following thresholds, as demonstrated by applicant-prepared estimates and utility/service provider documentation, including any phased expansion approved or constructed within five (5) years: 1. Water demand: average daily water demand > 100 gallons per minute (gpm); 2. Sanitary sewer: average daily sanitary discharge > 50,000 gallons/day; 3. Electric demand: maximum contracted demand or designed peak demand > 10 MW (or equivalent documented kW); 4. Hazardous materials / regulated wastes: storage, use, or generation requiring reporting under [EPCRA Tier II and/or applicable state hazardous materials reporting] and/or generation of hazardous waste at a level regulated under [state/federal hazardous waste generator requirements], as documented on a materials inventory submitted with the application. C. Exclusions. HRDF does not include general warehousing/distribution, general manufacturing, or office uses unless the Planning Commission determines, based on operational characteristics and supporting documentation, that the facility is substantially similar in operational profile to HRDF-type facilities (e.g., high-reliability power demand and continuous environmental control serving electronic/process loads) and meets subsections (A) and (B). D. Aggregation. CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF DELTA EATON COUNTY, MICHIGAN A RESOLUTION RECOGNIZING NOVEMBER 11, 2026 AS VETERANS DAY AND THE CONTRIBUTION OF VETERANS TO THE DELTA TOWNSHIP COMMUNITY WHEREAS, Veterans Day is observed annually on November 11 and traces its origins to the Armistice that ended World War I on November 11, 1918, a day set aside to honor the courage, sacrifice, and service of all the men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces; and WHEREAS, throughout our nation’s history, generations of Americans have answered the call to serve, defending the principles of freedom, democracy, and justice upon which our country was founded; and WHEREAS, the veterans of Delta Township represent a proud tradition of service and sacrifice, having served during times of war and peace in every branch of the United States military, and their dedication has helped preserve the liberties enjoyed by all Americans; and WHEREAS, military service requires extraordinary commitment, often demanding long separations from family, personal sacrifice, and great risk in defense of our nation and its interests; and WHEREAS, the strength and character demonstrated by our veterans continues long after their military service ends, as they remain active contributors to our community through public service, volunteerism, leadership, business development, civic engagement, mentorship, and support for fellow veterans; and WHEREAS, Delta Township recognizes the importance of supporting veterans and military families by fostering a welcoming community, honoring their service, and ensuring they have access to the respect, resources, and opportunities they have earned through their sacrifice; and WHEREAS, Veterans Day provides an opportunity for residents of all ages to reflect upon the sacrifices made by our nation’s veterans and to express gratitude for their service and dedication to protecting the freedoms we enjoy every day; and WHEREAS, the Delta Township Board wishes to formally recognize and thank all veterans, especially those residing within our community, whose courage, honor, and commitment have strengthened both our nation and our Township. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Delta Township Board hereby recognizes November 11, 2026, as Veterans Day in Delta Township and encourages all residents to pause in honor and appreciation of the brave men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Delta Township Board extends its deepest gratitude to all veterans for their selfless service, unwavering dedication, and countless sacrifices made in defense of our nation. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Delta Township Board reaffirms its commitment to honoring and supporting veterans and military families and recognizes the invaluable contributions they continue to make to the quality of life, civic spirit, and strength of the Delta Township community and our country. Brewer and the Delta Township Board From: Brian Reed, Township Manager Courtney Nicholls, Finance Director Date: October 5, 2026 Subject: Sheriff’s Contract Funding – Special Assessment Public Hearings In 2025 the Township levied a special assessment to pay for public safety services as allowed by Public Act 33 of 1951. This was done in response to the increase in costs necessary to renew the Township’s polices services agreement with the Eaton County Sheriff. The rate that was used was equivalent to 1.5 mills or $1.50 per thousand dollars of taxable value on real property in the Township. This type of assessment is not levied on properties that qualify for tax exemptions, including those for eligible disabled veterans, churches or schools. Staff has a presentation on the continuation of the special assessment, after which the board will hold public hearings and be asked to take action on two resolutions. The process is as follows - Presentation - Open public hearing on establishing the special assessment district - Consider resolution establishing the district o Suggested motion – I move that the Delta Township Board adopt the resolution to establish the 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District - If the resolution passes, open public hearing on setting the special assessment roll - Consider resolution setting the assessment roll o Suggested motion – I move that the Delta Township Board adopt the resolution to set the 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District Assessment Roll o If the Board would like to reduce the project cost in the resolution from $2,842,617 (Assessment roll) to $2,653,109 (Assessment Roll) (equivalent of 1.5 mills to the equivalent of 1.4 mills) there are two areas of the budget that can be updated to accommodate this. If the resolution is adopted at the lower amount these changes will be made to the budget for the budget public hearing on October 19. ▪ Following the last Board meeting we received notification that we received a FEMA grant for fire inspection, which will offset $100,000 in salary for a Fire Captain ▪ $100,000 was included in the budget as a placeholder for the Clement Underhill Drain – this can be removed if there is no interest in doing that project ▪ Staff is supportive of this action with the understanding that a conversation about funding long term needs of the Township (pension funding, building maintenance/updates, existing asset maintenance, staffing needs, purchase of fire trucks/ambulances, etc) will be discussed at the upcoming strategic planning session. 7710 West Saginaw Highway • Lansing, Michigan 48917-9712 Phone: (517) 323-8500 • Fax: (517) 323-8599 www.deltami.gov • www.facebook.com/deltatownship • www.twitter.com/deltatownship Back To Agenda Outline of process: 1. The Township Board adopts a resolution regarding its intent to move forward with the special assessment, and to conduct public hearings regarding the project, the proposed special assessment district and the special assessment roll – August 3, 2026 2. Notice of the public hearings must be published twice before the public hearing and also mailed (once) to every property owner in the special assessment district. 3. The public hearings are conducted. October 5, 2026 4. After the public hearings, either at that same Township Board meeting or at a subsequent Township Board meeting, the Township Board needs to adopt resolutions that confirm the special assessment district, project and special assessment roll. 5. The assessment is then placed on the winter tax bill. 7710 West Saginaw Highway • Lansing, Michigan 48917-9712 Phone: (517) 323-8500 • Fax: (517) 323-8599 www.deltami.gov • www.facebook.com/deltatownship • www.twitter.com/deltatownship A regular meeting of the Township Board of Trustees (the “Township Board”) of the Charter Township of Delta, Eaton County, Michigan (the “Township”), was held in Public Meeting Room A at the Delta Township Administration Building, 7710 West Saginaw Highway, Lansing, Michigan, on Monday, the 5th day of October, 2026, at 6:00 o'clock in the p.m. (the “Meeting”). Present: Absent: The following preamble and resolution were offered by ___ and supported by ___: WHEREAS, pursuant to the provisions of Act 33, Public Acts of Michigan, 1951, as amended (“Public Act 33”) and related Michigan law, the Township Board has tentatively approved the acquisition and undertaking of certain public safety activities and services, as well as other necessary and related public safety costs (the “Project”), and the establishment of a special assessment district therefor, for the purpose of defraying the cost of the Project, which Project and proposed special assessment district are further described in this resolution; and WHEREAS, the Township Board did meet in Public Meeting Room A at the Delta Township Administration Building, 7710 West Saginaw Highway, Lansing, Michigan, on Monday, the 5th day of October, 2026, at 6:00 o’clock, p.m., the time, date, and place set by the Township Board to conduct a public hearing to hear any objections to the Project, the costs and expenses of the Project, and the question of creating a special assessment district and defraying the costs and expenses of the Project by special assessment on the property to be especially benefited by the Project within the proposed special assessment district; and WHEREAS, plans and estimates of the costs and expenses of the Project are on file with the Township Clerk, and have been since September 15, 2026. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT: 1. The Township Board hereby determines to make, acquire, and undertake the following described public safety activities and services with respect to all lots and parcels of land within the Township that are subject to a special assessment pursuant to Public Act 33 and related Michigan law, referred to herein as the “2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District”: Public safety services and operation costs, including a portion of the cost of contracting for law enforcement services from the Eaton County Sheriff’s Office, as well as other necessary and related public safety costs (the “Project”) 2. The Township Board finally determines that the 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District for the Project shall be established as follows: the 2026 Public Safety Special Back to Memo Assessment District shall consist of all lots and parcels of land within the Charter Township of Delta that are subject to a special assessment pursuant to Public Act 33 and related Michigan law. 3. The Township Board hereby approves the plans and estimates of the costs and expenses for the Project as presented to the Township Board and on file with the Township Clerk, and determines to assess the full amount of such costs and expenses against the benefitting properties, lots, parcels of land within the 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District that are subject to a special assessment pursuant to Public Act 33 and related Michigan law. 4. All resolutions and parts of resolutions insofar as they conflict with the provisions of this resolution be, and the same are, hereby rescinded. Ayes: Nays: Absent: Resolution declared adopted. ___ Mary R. Present: Absent: The following preamble and resolution were offered by ___ and supported by ___: WHEREAS, pursuant to due notice to all interested parties, the Township Board met on Monday, October 5, 2026, in Public Meeting Room A at the Delta Township Administration Building, 7710 West Saginaw Highway, Lansing, Michigan, for the purpose of reviewing the proposed special assessment roll (the “Roll”) and conducting a public hearing regarding the Roll and hearing any objections thereto, for the 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District (the “Special Assessment District”); and WHEREAS, at the time and place designated for the meeting, the meeting was duly called to order and the Township Supervisor announced the opening of the hearing for objections to the proposed Roll on file with the Township Clerk, the Roll assessing, within the Special Assessment District, the cost of certain public safety activities and services, as well as other necessary and related public safety costs (the “Costs”) against the benefitting properties in the Special Assessment District; and WHEREAS, objections were heard or filed in writing with the Township Clerk and the following adjustments or corrections, if any, were made: ; and WHEREAS, the Township Board now desires to confirm the Roll as attached hereto as Exhibit A. All resolutions and parts of resolutions insofar as they conflict with the provisions of this resolution be, and the same are, hereby rescinded. Clark, Township Clerk EXHIBIT A [attach 2026 Public Safety Special Assessment District Special Assessment Roll] • Assessment Roll - $2,842,617 • Assessment Roll - $2,653,109 Proposed Public Safety Special Assessment How Did We Get Here?  Knowing they were facing serious financial challenges Eaton County put two millage proposals in front of the voters  November 3, 2024 – Passed in Delta/failed countywide  Tax limitation increase that would have allowed an additional levy of up to 3 mills  May 6, 2025 – Passed in Delta/failed countywide  Public safety millage proposal that would have allowed an additional levy of up to 2 mills  September 2, 2025  Board adopted public safety special assessment which was on the Winter 2025 tax bill How Did We Get Here?  The special assessment was needed to pay for the police contract thereby preserving the level of our other services, most importantly Fire and EMS services.  Without the assessment layoffs would have been necessary to generate the $2.8 million that was needed to fund the contract for police services.  The Township has protections in the contract that if the county does a public safety millage in the future, we will reopen our contract to more beneficial cost sharing. New Contract  The new contract that was approved by both the County and the Township has been in effect since October 1, 2025  Changes to the contract cost for 2026-2027  Reduction in payment to MERS for command staff from 135.91% of salary to 107.55% of salary  Reduced due to the one-time contribution made by the Township which is being paid back to the Township over ten years with interest and aggressive extra payments by the county  Addition of school resource officer  Waverly Schools will be paying the Township $150,000 per year for this position Township Budget  The draft 2027 budget shows the contract being paid in the following manner: Funding Source Amount Percentage Waverly Schools $150,000 1.9% General Fund $3,054,700 37.7% Public Safety Millage $2,058,500 25.4% Public Safety Assessment $2,840,000 35% Township Budget  Cuts were made to the 2026 budget to offset $1 million of the cost of the contract in General Fund. In 2027 several projects were not funded to keep the assessment at the equivalent of 1.5 mills. Capital Item Estimated Amount Resurfacing at Delta Center Cemetery $80,000 Resurfacing at Recycle Center $100,000+ Fire Station 1 Improvements $300,000 Hawk Meadow Bridge Replacement $200,000 Players Club Parking Lot/Drainage Unknown Community Center/Admin Bldg/ Enrichment Center Improvements Unknown – likely $500,000+ Proposed Special Assessment  To continue to fund a portion of the increased cost of the contract the Township is proposing the continuation of the public safety special assessment district.  Two public hearings will be held  One to set the district and one to set the roll  Notices were mailed to all property owners and published in the paper  Average cost of the special assessment for residents: $168.16 which is equivalent to $14 per month.  With this increase, Delta Township will continue to have a lower millage rate than the majority of surrounding communities; many of whom do not have full time police/fire/paramedic services.
