Stanford AICP, PEM Principal Planner Martha Haglund AICP Principal Planner Abby Carrigan Planning Intern Department Information TO: Marion Township Planning Commission FROM: Martha Haglund, AICP, Principal Planner DATE: October 13, 2026 SUBJECT: Special Land Use Permit- Section 17.33 Agricultural-Based Tourism/ Entertainment Activities (Agri-Business): Legacy Acres LOCATION: 775 Sexton Howell, 48843 (4710-14-300-009) Background/Location The applicant is seeking a Special Use Permit for Agri-Business. The property is located on 9.79 acres on the south side of Sexton Rd. west of Wolf Rd. and approximately a half mile west of D-19. The application describes the subject area as a previous horse farm with many of the same buildings and structures that currently exist. The Agri-Business is a sustainable livestock and agricultural education center hosting a variety of livestock such as alpacas, goats, rabbits and chickens. No additional structures or changes to the site plans are being proposed. Agri-business is a permitted special use in the Rural Residential and Suburban Residential Districts. Administration Building 304 E. Grand River Ave. Suite 206 • (517) 546-7555 Fax (517) 552-2347 • Web Site Milivcounty.com/planning Subject Site At the September Planning Commission Meeting Planning Staff reviewed the application for compliance with 17.33 Special Use Agricultural-Based Tourism October 13, 2026 Special Use Permit: Agri-Business: Legacy Acres Page: 2 /Entertainment. There were several outstanding items that the Planning Commission agreed needed to be addressed. The applicant has submitted a descriptive narrative and site plan. We offer the following for the Planning Commission’s review. 1. Provide a site plan that demonstrates how the facility will provide for circulation, parking, sanitation, trash collection, and noise, potential traffic impacts created by the proposed use and other factors during the events. • Traffic Circulation: The application specifies cars will enter property from Sexton Rd. and utilize internal driveways to park in the overflow parking area. There will not be vehicles queuing onto Sexton Rd. Planner Comment: Traffic circulation is compliant • Parking: The site plan designates 19,500 square feet for parking area on natural surface. The site plan does not specify drive lanes or spaces on the site plan. Calculating parking spaces, accounting for potentially two 18-foot drive lanes and average 200 square feet for each parking space this would allow for 69 parking spaces in that area. However, there does appear to be space for overflow parking south of the designated parking area on the site plan. The supplemental information specifies a maximum number of 80 vehicles to accommodate a peak event of maximum 100 individuals during a seasonal or holiday event. The information also describes there will not be off-street parking or need for employee parking. The application notes hosting groups 2-3 times a week but does not specify how large the average group will be. Planner Comment: The Planning Commission may consider reducing the number of parking spaces to fit in the designated area on the site plan. Additionally, the applicant should specify in writing what the average group size would be so the Planning Commission can better understand the traffic and parking implications. • Sanitation: Existing facilities in the guest house and pool house will be utilized for restrooms. For larger events portable toilets may be used. The application states that the agribusiness will be serviced by three residential refuse bins. Planner Comment: The Planning Commission may ask applicant to identify where portable toilets would be placed on the site and identify them on the site plan. • Noise: The application describes the agribusiness will produce noise such as animal sounds, farm equipment, and normal conversation. The application also states there could be 4-6 large seasonal events a year that may have amplified music and speaker system between the hours of 9-9:00 PM that will be located within the central portion of the property and designated areas on the site plan. October 13, 2026 Special Use Permit: Agri-Business: Legacy Acres Page: 3 Planner Comment: The Planning Commission should consider if this is appropriate and reasonable. The Planning Commission can regulate frequency or times of the week of these events. The Planning Commission may want to confirm no amplified music will be played at the pool or pool house since it is not located in the central portion of the site. 2. Provide a site plan with setbacks and building dimensions. The building dimensions are described in a table and site plan includes setbacks. Planner Comment: The application is compliant 3. Provide a site plan that represents what portion of the structures will be used for agribusiness in relation to the whole site. The application specifies which structures will be used for private, primary agriculture, and agribusiness. The small livestock barn (960 sq ft), large barn lean-to (1,800 sq ft), guesthouse (800 sq ft) and pool house (200 sq ft) will be the structures used for agribusiness. Planner Comment: The application is complete and compliant. 4. Provide documentation that the total floor area above finished grade (one or two stories) of any agri-business facility falling into this category, including retail space, is no larger than 10,000 square feet. The application includes a table noting the above structures total 3,760 sq ft. Planner Comment: The applicant is compliant. 5. Provide a site plan or description of what structures or areas are private, primary agriculture or agribusiness. Planner Comment: Applicant is compliant (See #3 above) 6. Provide more detailed information about frequency of programming and type of events. The application details hosting groups 2-3 times a week with the occasional larger events 46 times a year with a maximum group size of 100 individuals. Planner Comment: The applicant should specify in writing the average size group. 7. If applicable, provide more information about proposed signage and demonstrate compliance with 15.5 (B) Farm Signs. Planner Comment: No signs are proposed; this requirement is not applicable. 8. Approval of all governing agencies including but not limited to Howell Area Fire Authority, Livingston County Road Commission, Health Department, Livingston County Drain Commission. October 13, 2026 Special Use Permit: Agri-Business: Legacy Acres Page: 4 The application states that because there aren’t site changes or earth moving that the applicant doesn’t believe the proposal triggers separate permits or approvals from every agency. Planner Comment: It should be noted that approval of governing agencies can be completed administratively following the decision from the Township. The proposed special use must be reviewed/approved by all governing agencies. Section 16.05 Basis for Determination Must consider the following criteria when determining a special land use. 1. Be harmonious with and in accordance with the general principles and objectives of the Comprehensive Plan of the Township. Throughout the Township Master Plan, it highlights the importance of agriculture preservation including on Page 61 Goal 19, “Keep farming a viable and visible part of Marion Township’s future land use plan. Open Space green way and farmland preservation should be of the highest priority.” The agricultural use is in accordance with the principals and objectives of the Township Master Plan. 2. Be designed, constructed, operated and maintained so as to be harmonious and appropriate in appearance with the existing or intended character of the general vicinity and that such a use will not change the essential character of the area in which it is proposed. The proposed agribusiness will be harmonious and appropriate with the existing rural residential and adjacent agricultural uses. There are some outstanding items from Section 17.33 that can help ensure the agribusiness will be operated and maintained to be compatible with the surrounding area. 3. Not be hazardous or disturbing to existing or future uses in the same general vicinity and will substantially improve property in the immediate vicinity and in the community as a whole. Agricultural programming will not be hazardous or disturbing to existing or future uses in the same general vicinity. 4. Be served adequately by essential public facilities and services, such as highways, streets, police, fire protection, drainage structures, refuse disposal, water and sewage facilities and schools. The site is served by private well and septic and will be adequately served by essential public facilities. 5. Not involve uses, activities, processes, materials and equipment or conditions of operation that will be detrimental to any person, property or general welfare by reason of excessive production of traffic, noise, smoke, fumes, glare or odors. It does not appear the agribusiness proposal will produce conditions that will be detrimental to any person, property or general welfare. The Planning Commission should determine if the proposal’s traffic, parking or frequency of events is appropriate and reasonable. October 13, 2026 Special Use Permit: Agri-Business: Legacy Acres Page: 5 6. Meet the intent and purpose of the zoning regulations; be related to the standards established in the Ordinance for the land use or activity under consideration; and will be in compliance with these standards. The use aligns with the intent of the Township Zoning Regulations. The applicant has addressed many of the outstanding items from the September staff report. 7. Ensure that landscaping shall be preserved in its natural state, insofar as practicable, by minimizing tree and soil removal, and by topographic modifications, which result in maximum harmony with adjacent areas. No changes are proposed and the applications states, “The existing barns, pastures, fencing and open spaces continue to serve agricultural purposes while preserving the property’s farming heritage.” The existing agricultural structures and landscape will be compatible with adjacent properties. 8. Ensure that special attention shall be given to proper site surface drainage so that removal of storm waters will not adversely affect neighboring properties. The application notes, “Existing grading and drainage patterns will remain in place, so adjacent properties ware not adversely affected.” The Planning Commission may request additional information about the existing conditions and request a topographic map of the site. The findings reviewed from Section 16.05 of the Township Zoning ordinance generally support the proposed special land use for Agribusiness at 225 Sexton Rd. Howell. Planning Commission Recommendation Planning Staff recommends approval of the special use conditional on the following items: 1. Reduce parking spaces from 80 to 69 or indicate an area for overflow parking on site plan. 2. Provide the average group number that would be in attendance 2-3 times a week. 3. Any other documentation requested from the Township Planning Commission. 4. Approval of all governing agencies including but not limited to Howell Area Fire Authority, Livingston County Health Department, Livingston County Road Commission, Livingston County Drain Commission. A Planning Commission recommendation to the Township Board should be based on the findings from Section 16.05 and compliance with Section 17.33. The Planning Commission may make a recommendation to the Township Board to approve, approve with conditions or deny the Special Use Permit. If additional information is required, the Planning Commission may postpone action and allow the applicant more time to provide requested information. LEGACY ACRES | 775 SEXTON ROAD | MARION TOWNSHIP Legacy Acres Supplemental Response Special Use Permit for Agricultural Based Tourism and Entertainment Activities Applicants Troy and Britney Hoskins Property 775 Sexton Road, Howell, Michigan 48843 Parcel 10-14-300-009 (Livingston County full ID: 4710-14300-009) Review Livingston County Department of Planning memorandum dated August 17, 2026 Submitted September 9, 2026 Purpose of This Response This supplement responds to the outstanding items identified in the County planning review and should be read with the original application and Existing Conditions Site Plan. Legacy Acres will use existing buildings, pastures, parking, access, utilities, grading, and drainage. No new construction or material site alteration is proposed. The requested use remains incidental to the working farm. Agriculture, livestock care, poultry and egg production, fiber production, gardening, and land stewardship will remain the principal uses of the property. Response to Planning Review Items 1 Site Operations and Potential Impacts Circulation and parking. The designated guest parking and overflow parking areas were included on the originally submitted site plan and are reiterated here for clarity. Guests will enter through the existing driveway on Sexton Road and park entirely on-site. The horseshoe driveway allows vehicles to circulate and turn around without backing onto Sexton Road. The designated parking field can accommodate approximately 80 vehicles. No roadside parking, paved parking area, new driveway, or change to the existing access is proposed. Transportation. Transportation will vary by program. Schools, youth groups, and community organizations may arrive through carpooling, passenger vans, or buses, reducing the number of individual vehicles. Other visitors may arrive in individual cars. Vehicles will not queue or park along Sexton Road. Staff parking. Legacy Acres is currently family-operated. Family members park in the existing garage, so no additional employee parking is required. If nonresident staff are added later, they will use designated on-site parking. Supplemental Response to Planning Review | 1 LEGACY ACRES | 775 SEXTON ROAD | MARION TOWNSHIP Restrooms. Visitors will have access to existing restroom facilities in the guesthouse and pool house. For larger scheduled groups, portable restrooms may be added as needed to supplement the existing facilities and improve efficiency. Trash collection. Legacy Acres maintains three residential trash bins. Visitor waste will be collected in designated containers and transferred to the existing bins for regular disposal. Larger programs may use additional temporary waste containers as needed. Noise. Routine programming will involve normal conversation, agricultural instruction, animal interaction, and ordinary farm sounds. A DJ or speaker system may occasionally be used during larger holiday or seasonal agricultural events. Page 5 To: Planning Commission From: Brian Shorkey, Principal Planner Date: October 12, 2026 Re: Special Use Permit #26035 (Bridges Care and Education Center), establish group child care home for up to twelve children at 2990 Briarcliff Drive. Abhirami Gunasingam (Applicant) has requested a special use permit to operate a group child care home for up to 14 children at 2990 Briarcliff Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823 (Subject Property). The 0.4-acre site is zoned RAA (Single Family–Low Density). The applicant currently operates a family child care home, known as Bridges Care and Education Center, on the Subject Property. Sec. 86-654 of the Code of Ordinances allows group child care homes as non-residential special uses in a residential zoning district subject to special use permit (SUP) approval. In accordance with the Child Care Organizations Act (Public Act 116 of 1973), the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), Child Care Licensing Division, regulates child care facilities based on the number of children under supervision. A facility caring for less than six children is defined as a family child care home and is not subject to local zoning laws. Facilities with greater than six children, with a maximum of 12, are defined as group child care homes and are subject to local zoning approval. PA 106 of 2022 amended the state’s child care regulations to allow group child care homes to increase their capacity to 14 children if certain criteria are fulfilled. Zoning and Future Land Use The Subject Property is located in the RAA – Single-Family Residential zoning district. The same zoning designation applies to all surrounding adjacent properties. The RAA district requires a minimum of 90 feet of lot frontage and 13,500 square feet of lot area for new lots. The Subject Property totals approximately 0.41 acre in size. The Subject Property has a total of approximately 178 feet of frontage along Briarcliff Drive. The Subject Property conforms to the RAA zoning district. ZONING MAP Special Use Permit #26035 (Bridges Care and Education Center) Planning Commission Page 2 The Future Land Use Map from the 2023 Master Plan designates the Subject Property in the Suburban Residential category. The same designation applies to all surrounding adjacent properties. The Suburban Residential designation correlates with the RAA Zoning District. Physical Features The subject property is developed with an approximate 1,800 square foot singlefamily house. The rear yard has a fencedin play area, approximately 2,500 square feet, that has been reviewed and approved by the State of Michigan. There are no wetland or floodplain issues. FUTURE LAND USE Streets & Traffic The site has frontage and access on Briarcliff Drive. Briarcliff Drive is two lanes wide and classified as a local street. Parking is allowed on Briarcliff Drive and the Subject Property has a paved pullout in front of the yard, next to the driveway. The daily process for pick-up and drop-off traffic at the subject site starts at 8:00 am and ends at 5:30 pm. The nearest major street with access to Briarcliff Drive is Hagadorn Road. Staff Analysis The Township’s Code of Ordinances allows a group child care home as a nonresidential use in a residential zoning district, subject to Special Use Permit approval. The proposed group child care home will operate between the hours of 8:00 am and 6:00 pm, Monday through Friday. According to the applicant, two staff members, the owners of the subject site, will be on-site at all times during operation. One employee is expected to be hired to work between 8:00 am and 6:00 pm. The Applicant has applied for a license from the State of Michigan to operate a group child care home. Prior to issuing a license, LARA inspects the property for such items as outdoor play area and equipment, water hazards, home maintenance and safety, utility service, ventilation, lighting, exit and escape requirements, smoke detectors, and emergency plans. Michigan Zoning Enabling Act The Michigan Zoning Enabling Act (the “MZEA,” Public Act 110 of 2006) requires the Township to issue a special use permit for a group child care home if it meets all the following standards 1. The group child care home is located no closer than 1,500 feet, as measured along a public street, to a) another licensed group child care home b) an adult foster care small group home or large group home licensed under the adult foster care facility licensing act c) a facility offering substance abuse treatment and rehabilitation service to 7 or more people d) A community Providing a safe and welcoming, sustainable, prime community. Has appropriate fencing for the safety of the children in the group child care home as determined by the local unit of government. CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF MERIDIAN REGULAR MEETING PLANNING COMMISSION 5000 Okemos Road, Okemos MI 48864-1198 517.853.4000, Township Townhall Room Monday, September 21, 2026, 6:30 pm PRESENT: Chair Romback, Vice-Chair McCurtis, Commissioners Brooks, Shrewsbury, and Nahum STAFF: Principal Planner Shorkey ABSENT: Commissioner McConnell 1. CALL MEETING TO ORDER Chair Romback called the September 21, 2026, regular meeting for the Meridian Township Planning Commission to order at 6:32 pm. 2. ROLL CALL Chair Romback called the roll of the Board. All Board members were present except for Commissioner McConnell. 3. PUBLIC REMARKS None 4. APPROVAL OF AGENDA Vice-Chair McCurtis moved to approve the September 21, 2026, Regular Planning Commission meeting agenda as amended. Seconded by Commissioner Brooks. Motion passed unanimously. 5. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Commissioner Nahum moved to approve Minutes of the August 10, 2026 meeting as amended. Seconded by Vice-Chair McCurtis. Motion passed unanimously. 6. COMMUNICATIONS Principal Planner Shorkey pointed out the communication from Bath Township regarding their Master Plan update. Commissioner Brooks said that the link on the communication did not include the draft Master Plan. Shorkey said that he would contact Bath Township for the correct link. 7. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. PUD #26026 – Capstone Hannah Boulevard Apartments Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet. Shorkey pointed out the updates to the plan since the rezoning application. Page 1 Vice-Chair McCurtis asked about a small wetland on the plan. Principal Planner Shorkey said that the wetland was 0.07 acre in size and unregulated. Chair Romback asked what the minimum was for a regulated wetland. Shorkey answered a quarter acre. Commissioner Brooks asked about required minimum parking. Principal Planner Shorkey discussed the parking calculations on the site plan and said the proposed calculations meet the parking ordinances. Discussion about parking on the project. Commissioner Brooks asked about stormwater. Principal Planner Shorkey said that the general Drain Commission standard was that stormwater did not leave the site. Brooks asked about the location of stormwater measures on the plan. Shorkey said that the Applicant’s engineer was present and could discuss. John Atkin of Capstone Communities addressed the Planning Commission and gave a presentation and discussed the proposed plan. Vice-Chair McCurtis asked about stormwater and the direction of grading. Greg Petru, engineer for the Applicant, discussed the stormwater mitigation for the proposed project and said that less water would go east. Commissioner Nahum asked about bike storage. Mr. Atkin said that storage was typically under stairwells. Commissioner Brooks asked about parking and asked Mr. Atkin to discuss how they calculated the number of parking spaces. Commissioner Nahum asked if the shuttle service would extend to the site. Commissioner Shrewsbury asked if the units were leased on a per room basis. Commissioner Brooks asked if this had originally been proposed as student housing and if they charged for parking. Vice-Chair McCurtis asked if there is extra parking for visitors. Chair Romback asked if there was a connection between the development and the neighborhood. Commissioner Brooks brought up the Master Plan goals and said that he was struggling with the scale of the parking lot and discussed alternative traffic options and asked if future building could be built. Principal Planner Shorkey said no and that the number of units for the site was capped. Mr. Atkin said that most of the parking is interior to the buildings like has been done on developments to the west. Commissioner Brooks asked if residents could be allowed to park on adjacent developments. Chair Romback opened the floor for public comment at 7:02; seeing no comment, Chair Romback immediately closed the floor. After a straw poll, the Planning Commission indicated support for the project. Principal Planner Shorkey said that based on the conversation, Staff would bring a resolution to recommend approval to the next meeting. B. SUP #26028 – New Hope Church Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet and described the attached plan. Commissioner Nahum asked what was taking place across Newton Road. Principal Planner Shorkey showed it on the map and said it was the former movie theater location. Commissioner Brooks asked how the driveway permit was issued and how that meant that a traffic study was not required. Principal Planner Shorkey said that the Road Department would not retroactively revoke their driveway permit and that the applicant had discussed their plan with the Road Department before the driveway permit was issued. Page 2 Chair Romback asked if the church was treated under other requirements or if it is treated like any other applicant. Principal Planner Shorkey confirmed that it was an SUP and under the usual regulations. Romback confirmed that the SUP application had to go to the Board for final approval because of the 25,000 square feet regulation and not because it is a church. Commissioner Nahum asked if further development could happen on the north part of the property where wetlands are located. Principal Planner Shorkey said further development could occur, but it would be difficult due to the wetlands. Commissioner Brooks asked about the minimum parking requirements for the building. Principal Planner Shorkey said that he did not go back and look at existing parking since it is already inadequate for the church’s needs. Shorkey said that he would have to do more figuring for the building addition. Brooks asked what was the maximum number of people that could occupy the building. Shorkey brought up the parking regulations and discussed the parking requirements for the site. Shorkey said that parking calculations would arrive during site plan approval. Brooks asked for parking calculations to be provided at the next meeting. Nathan Hebekeuser and Woody Isaacs, representing the applicant, addressed the Planning Commission and discussed the proposed plan. Mr. Isaacs spoke about conversations with the Road Department and said that they were satisfied with the engineering aspects of the driveway. Mr. Isaacs said that they had been talking with the Drain Commission’s office and was planning onsite retention. Mr. Hebekeuser said that next year, the drain was being extended to the site. Chair Romback asked about overflow parking and said that he would be hesitant to limit parking for a place of worship. Commissioner Nahum asked about the residence on the parcel. Mr. Hebekeuser said that was being used for storage. Chair Romback opened the floor for public comment at 7:21. Michael Bristor spoke in favor of SUP #26028. Sam Waldmiller spoke in favor of SUP #26028. Hearing no further comment, Chair Romback closed the floor at 7:28. After a straw poll, the Planning Commission indicated support for the project. Principal Planner Shorkey said that based on the conversation, Staff would bring a resolution to recommend approval to the next meeting. C. ZA #26025 – Professional Office Updates Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo in the packet. After a short discussion, Chair Romback opened the floor for public comment; seeing no comment, Chair Romback immediately closed the floor. After a straw poll, the Planning Commission indicated support for the project. Principal Planner Shorkey said that based on the conversation, Staff would bring a resolution to recommend approval to the next meeting. 8. UNFINISHED BUSINESS A. None 9. OTHER BUSINESS Page 3 A. CR #26033 – Section 61 Review – Township Property Acquisition – Liverance Street Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo and discussed the history of the application. Commissioner Nahum asked if there are structures on the property. Principal Planner Shorkey said there were but they should come down based on the prior site plan. Chair Romback asked if the owner was notified. Commissioner Shrewsbury asked if the Township would maintain or demolish the structure. Commissioner Shrewsbury asked about the market value and the proposed amount of the purchase. Principal Planner Shorkey discussed the appraisal and the purchase process. Commissioner Brooks said that the preservation makes sense from a land use perspective and asked what not owning this parcel does to future development potential. Shorkey discussed the past Okemos Village proposal and drainage in the area. Brooks asked about stormwater requirements in the area. Shorkey discussed potential stormwater mitigation in the area. Commissioner Nahum asked about the process and the next stages for approval. Principal Planner Shorkey said that the Board gives final approval. Chair Romback asked if the Commission could move to an immediate view. Commissioner Shrewsbury asked if there was an urgency to move on the application. Commissioner Nahum moved to recommend approval of CR #26033. Seconded by ViceChair McCurtis. Motion passed unanimously. B. CR #26034 – Section 61 Review – Township Property Acquisition – Algonquin Way Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo and discussed the history of the application. Commissioner Brooks asked about how much property the Township owns. Principal Planner Shorkey showed the map and confirmed. Commissioner Shrewsbury complemented the Township for purchasing properties like this for preservation. Commissioner Nahum moved to recommend approval of CR #26034. Seconded by Commissioner Brooks. Motion passed unanimously. C. Drive-Through Sign Review – Wendy’s Principal Planner Shorkey summarized the memo and explained the need for the application. Vice-Chair McCurtis moved to approve the drive-through signage for Wendy’s on Marsh Road. Seconded by Commissioner Brooks. Motion passed unanimously. Chair Romback asked when the requirement for this application was written. Principal Planner Shorkey said the sign ordinance was updated within the last four to five years. Romback said that the requirement for Planning Commission approval for drive-thru signage is an overstep and would like the Planning Commission to look at this language in the future. 10. REPORTS AND ANNOUNCEMENTS A. Township Board Update Principal Planner Shorkey updated the Planning Commission on recent Board activity. Page 4 B. Liaison Reports Commissioner Nahum discussed recent activity of the Zoning Board of Appeals. 11. PROJECT UPDATES None 12. PUBLIC REMARKS None 13. COMMISSIONER COMMENTS Principal Planner Shorkey informed the Planning Commission that the October 26 Planning Commission meeting would be held in the Central Fire Station. Vice-Chair McCurtis said that he would be unable to attend the October 12 Planning Commission meeting. Commissioner Brooks commented about road access in the Land Division act and suggested that the Land Division act said that you cannot cut off stub streets. Commissioner Brooks discussed parking and suggested that parking spaces are incentives and affect rent rates. Brooks said that the Township wants people to use buses and bikes but increasing parking spaces incentivizes traffic. Commissioner Nahum said that he in favor of reducing parking and incentivizing other modes of transportation. Discussion about parking and transportation ensued. 14. ADJOURNMENT Chair Romback called for a motion to adjourn the meeting. Commissioner Brooks moved to adjourn the September 21, 2026 regular meeting of the Planning Commission. Seconded by Commissioner Nahum. Motion passed unanimously at 8:16. To: Planning Commission From: Brian Shorkey, Principal Planner Date: October 26, 2026 Re: Special Use Permit #26035 (Bridges Care and Education Center), establish group child care home for up to twelve children at 2990 Briarcliff Drive. Abhirami Gunasingam (Applicant) has requested a special use permit to operate a group child care home for up to 14 children at 2990 Briarcliff Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823 (Subject Property). The 0.4-acre site is zoned RAA (Single Family–Low Density). The applicant currently operates a family child care home, known as Bridges Care and Education Center, on the Subject Property. Sec. 86-654 of the Code of Ordinances allows group child care homes as non-residential special uses in a residential zoning district subject to special use permit (SUP) approval. In accordance with the Child Care Organizations Act (Public Act 116 of 1973), the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), Child Care Licensing Division, regulates child care facilities based on the number of children under supervision. A facility caring for less than six children is defined as a family child care home and is not subject to local zoning laws. Facilities with greater than six children, with a maximum of 12, are defined as group child care homes and are subject to local zoning approval. PA 106 of 2022 amended the state’s child care regulations to allow group child care homes to increase their capacity to 14 children if certain criteria are fulfilled. Zoning and Future Land Use The Subject Property is located in the RAA – Single-Family Residential zoning district. The same zoning designation applies to all surrounding adjacent properties. The RAA district requires a minimum of 90 feet of lot frontage and 13,500 square feet of lot area for new lots. The Subject Property totals approximately 0.41 acre in size. The Subject Property has a total of approximately 178 feet of frontage along Briarcliff Drive. The Subject Property conforms to the RAA zoning district. Meeting Location: 5151 Marsh Road, Okemos, Ml 48864 Township Hall Providing a safe and welcoming, sustainable, prime community. 9.A CONSENT AGENDA BOARD COMMUNICATIONS From: To: Cc: Subject: Date: Christian & Beth Ann Bechtel Board Tim Dempsey; Dan Opsommer; Courtney Wisinski; Emma Campbell FYI: Meridian Township Goat Browsing Demonstration Event, Saturday, October 17, 2026 at 9:30am at Towar Woods Preserve Wednesday, September 30, 2026 11:39:59 AM Dear Meridian Township Board Members, For some time, I have been encouraging Meridian Township Board Members, Commissions Members, Advisory Board Members, and Staff Employees to seek natural and healthy holistic care to maintain our township preserves, parks, athletic fields, etc. I have come to prior board, commission and advisory meetings with public comments asking you all and sharing resources, for protecting our health, to please forge new path commitments towards reducing and eventually eliminating all township toxic synthetic chemicals use for the benefit of staff employees' and residents' health. Board Members and Staff Employees have been listening, open to natural healthy ways, and an effort has been made toward this goal. I am thankful and full of gratitude that on Saturday, October 17, 2026 at 9:30am at Meridian Township Towar Woods Preserve, Meridian Township Conservation Corps is co-leading a Goat Browsing Demonstration Event with local Okemos based non-profit Mid-Michigan Land Conservancy who is bringing goats to demonstrate how Goats Browsing naturally and healthily reduces invasive plants species. Non-profit Wild Ones Red Cedar Chapter is also partnering with this Goat Browsing Demonstration Event. See weblinks below: Meridian Township Goat Browsing/Grazing Demonstration Event (Saturday, 1017-2026 at 9:30am at Meridian Township Towar Woods Preserve, see weblinks for address details) a. https://events.meridian.mi.us/default/Detail/2026-10-17-0930-Goat-BrowsingDemonstration-Event b. https://www.midmilandcons.org/events-andactivities/ewr8y2sqytz8segnsvd2ki8up3p5kq c. https://www.facebook.com/events/3740371592789240/ d. https://wildoneslansing.weebly.com/wild-ones-red-cedar-chapterevents.html (Scroll down to October 17th) Managed targeted goats browsing is one effective natural strategy tool option that helps reduce invasive plant species such as Oriental Bittersweet, Japanese Knotweed, Kudzu, Buckthorn, Poison Ivy, etc. along with many other invasive plant species. Goats browsing key mechanisms are as follows: 1. Seed Control: Goats' digestive systems significantly reduce seed germination of many invasive plants, preventing them from spreading to new areas. 2. Improves Soil Health: As goats browse, their hooves loosen and break up compacted land while their manure provides natural fertilizer for native plant recovery. 3. Biomass Reduction: Goats intensive browsing significantly lowers the cover and the height of invasive shrubs, reducing competitive pressure on native plants. 4. Complementary Management: Goats browsing can be used with mechanical brush cutting, manual hand-pulling and/or controlled burns. Please Note: I have previously provided the Meridian Township Staff a list of Goatscaping Services that can be used as a resource going forward which includes reasonable Goatscaping Services here in our local area. I hope that Meridian Township Board and Staff Employees will welcome more natural Goatscaping Services in the future. Additionally, I am optimistic that all natural and holistic options will be used to safeguard our health and continue moving forward with the ultimate goal of eliminating all township synthetic toxic chemical use. I hope to see you there on Saturday, October 17th at Meridian Township Towar Woods Preserve for this fun and educational Goats Browsing Demonstration Event. MERIDIAN: PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that any qualified elector who is not already registered, may register to vote at the office of the Meridian Township Clerk; the office of the County Clerk; a Secretary of State Branch Office, or other designated state agency. Qualified electors who have a valid Michigan driver’s license or state ID, may register online at https://mvic.sos.state.mi.us/. Registration forms may be obtained at mi.gov/vote and mailed or dropped off at the office of the Meridian Township Clerk. Voters who are already registered may update their registration at www.expressSOS.com. The last day to register in any manner other than in-person with the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office is Monday, October 19, 2026. After this date, anyone who qualifies as an elector must register to vote in person with proof of residency (MCL 168.492) at the following location and times: Meridian Township Clerk’s Office - 5151 Marsh Road, Okemos, MI 48864 • Regular Business Hours: Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. • Saturday, October 31st and Sunday, November 1st from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. • Election Day, Tuesday, November 3rd from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that Meridian Township will hold a General Election on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. For the purposes of electing candidates for the following office: • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • GOVERNOR AND LIEUTENTANT GOVERNOR SECRETARY OF STATE ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES SENATOR REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS STATE SENATOR REPRESENTATIVE IN STATE LEGISLATURE MEMBER OF THE STATE BOARD OF EDUCATION REGENT OF THE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN TRUSTEE OF MICHIGAN STATE UNIVERSITY GOVERNOR OF WAYNE STATE UNIVERSITY TOWNSHIP TREASURER JUSTICE OF SUPREME COURT JUDGE OF COURT OF APPEALS – 4TH DISTRICT – INCUMBENT POSITION JUDGE OF CIRCUIT COURT – 30TH CIRCUIT – INCUMBENT POSITION – 6 YEAR TERM JUDGE OF CIRCUIT COURT – 30TH CIRCUIT – INCUMBENT POSITION – PARTIAL TERM ENDING 01/01/2029 JUDGE OF PROBATE COURT – INGHAM COUNTY JUDGE OF DISTRICT COURT – 55TH DISTRICT – INCUMBENT POSITION BOARD OF TRUSTEES MEMBER – LANSING COMMUNITY COLLEGE LOCAL SCHOOL DISTRICT BOARD MEMBER For the purposes of voting on the following proposals as listed below: • • PROPOSAL 2026-1 A PROPOSAL TO COVENE A CONSTITUTIONAL CONVENTION FOR THE PURPOSE OF DRAFTING A GENERAL REVISION OF THE STATE CONSTITUTION PROPOSAL 2026-2 A PROPSED INITATED LAW TO PROHIBIT CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF MERIDIAN, INGHAM COUNTY LEGAL AD NOTICE: NOTICE OF REGISTRATION FOR THE NOVEMBER 3, 2026, GENERAL ELECITON • • FROM CERTAIN REGULATED UTILITIES AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS AND APPLY CAMPAIGN FINANCE LAWS AND REGULATIONS TO ADDITIONAL TYPES OF POLITICAL COMMUNICATIONS CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF MERIDIAN PARK MILLAGE RENEWAL CHARTER TOWNSHIP OF MERIDIAN POLICE AND FIRE PROTECTION MILLAGE RENEWAL The full text of the ballot proposals and sample ballots can be found at www.mi.gov/vote or can be viewed at the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office, 5151 Marsh Road, Okemos, MI 48864. Persons with disabilities needing accommodations should contact the Clerk’s Office. ABSENT VOTER BALLOTS: Any registered voter may request an Absent Voter Ballot. The Meridian Township Clerk’s Office must have a signed application to issue an Absent Voter Ballot. You may apply online at www.mi.gov/vote or at the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office. Monday, November 2, 2026, at 4 pm is the deadline to request an absentee ballot in person, except for those who register to vote on Election Day. Those registering to vote on Election Day, November 3, 2026, are eligible to receive an Absent Voter Ballot at the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office. EARLY VOTING CENTER All qualified electors in the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office have the option to vote early in person, beginning Saturday, October 24th through Sunday, November 1st, 2026 from 9:00 AM until 5:00 PM daily. The Early Voting Center will be held at the Meridian Township Municipal Building – 5151 Marsh Road, Okemos, MI 48864. Providing a safe and welcoming, sustainable, prime comm resident, or associated meeting notes over a finite one-year period is a standard, narrow request. It is legally untenable to argue that a thirteen-dollar administrative expenditure creates an "unreasonably high cost" or severe operational hardship for Meridian Township. 2. Staff Interruption is Not a Valid Fee Justification: Fulfilling FOIA requests is, by definition, a core statutory duty of the Township. Claiming a request creates a high cost because it "takes time away from other duties" attempts to convert a routine public service into a financial penalty for the requester. If general workplace interruption were the legal standard, the statutory limitation on labor charges would be completely nullified. 3. The 4-Hour Redaction Estimate is Unsubstantiated: You have estimated 4 hours of redaction labor for a pool of records that takes only 30 minutes to pull. This is a disproportionate ratio. Furthermore, under Michigan FOIA, labor for redaction can only be charged if the redactions are required by law(exemptions that are mandatory, not permissive). I request a written clarification detailing exactly what legally mandatory exemptions apply to a narrow, one-year electronic search that would necessitate 4 hours of legal review. Requested Remedy: Pursuant to MCL § 15.234(10), I request that the Township Board or FOIA Coordinator review this matter and waive the labor fees entirely, as they fail to meet the statutory threshold of "unreasonably high costs." If the Township maintains that a 30-minute electronic search constitutes an unreasonable financial hardship under the law, please provide the specific, written legal justification and factual findings supporting this determination, as required to preserve the record for potential judicial review under MCL § 15.235. Thank you for your prompt attention to this statutory appeal. text: TOWNSHIP BOARD MEETING TUESDAY, OCTOBER 13, 2026 Welcome to the Napoleon Township Board Meeting. We appreciate your attendance. Board Members receive their packets in advance, allowing an opportunity to prepare for the meeting and be ready to conduct the business of the Township efficiently. Our meetings usually finish in less than an hour. Before the meeting starts, please turn off or mute all electronic devices. Our meeting will proceed according to the agenda that follows. The first public comment is limited to items on the agenda and is for a maximum of 2 minutes per person and 10 minutes per subject. After a non-routine motion is made by the Board, seconded, and discussed, the Supervisor may ask for public comment before the formal vote of the Board is taken. Comments are limited to 2 minutes per person. The last public comment is open for any Township business to be addressed and is limited to 2 minutes per person. For all public comment, please stand and state your full name and residence address. All comments are directed to the Township Board. Thank you for your interest in Napoleon Township. We hope to see you at future meetings. Please Note: During public comment the Board does not answer questions and does not engage in discussion or debate with the person making the comment. DAN WYMER SUPERVISOR TRACI SPRING CLERK ANITA GRAHAM TREASURER JOHN HUMMER TRUSTEE JULIE STAGE TRUSTEE NAPOLEON TOWNSHIP TOWNSHIP HALL 6755 Brooklyn Rd Napoleon, MI www.napoleontownship.us CALL TO ORDER 6:00 PM — TUESDAY, OCTOBER 13, 2026 PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE APPROVAL OF AGENDA Motion to Accept or Motion to Change CONSENT AGENDA Approval of Minutes - September 8 Regular Board Meeting September 8 Lakeview Special Assessment Public Hearing 1 Payment of Claims PUBLIC COMMENT - Agenda Items Only COUNTY COMMISSION REPORT —- Commissioner Kennedy DEPARTMENT MONTHLY REPORTS Fire Police Ordinance Enforcement Building & Zoning Assessing Sewer & Water Operations Planning Commission Zoning Board of Appeals NEW BUSINESS Bucket Brigade Contribution for Halloween Event Cooling Unit Replacement in Electrical Equipment Room Quarterly Budget Adjustment Josh’s Dumpster - Offer of Cleanup Events Data Centers - Discussion UNFINISHED BUSINESS UPDATES e Commuter Parking Area Marking by TRI-County Striping Commuter Parking Area Rules & Signage Wolf Lake Canal Weed Special Assessment — Resolution Continuing Process Lakeview Drive Road Special Assessment — Resolution Confirming Special Assessment Roll Crypt Roof Replacement — Donations Trail Cameras To Catch Dumpers Upcoming Election Tire Collection Event Unemployment Benefits Hearing Outcome Safety Concern - Floor Mats Replaced County Gravel Processing Resumes at Blue Ridge Pit PUBLIC COMMENT- Any Township Business Adjourn Minutes of Napoleon Township Regular Board Meeting September 8, 2026 Call to Order at 6:00 p.m. by Supervisor Wymer with members Graham, Hummer, Spring and Stage. Pledge of Allegiance APPROVAL OF AGENDA AND CONSENT AGENDA: Motion by Hummer, support by Stage to approve the agenda including the consent agenda, with the payment of claims GOF = $126,473.70 and Restricted = $72,831.89, and minutes of the August 11, 2026 regular board meeting as amended. Motion passed. PUBLIC COMMENT - AGENDA ITEMS ONLY: None COUNTY COMMISSIONER REPORT: No report provided by Commissioner Kennedy. DEPARTMENT MONTHLY REPORTS: Fire: Chief Bickford’s written report included 77 calls for service in August, 8 of which were in Norvell Township for a total of 590 calls year-to-date. Police: Chief Pittman reported 405 Central Dispatch calls for service and a total of 248 other investigations in August. Ordinance Enforcement: Jeff Kirkpatrick is working on complaints on Cady Road for a rooster, court-ordered cleanups on Flagstar and Thru Roamin, search warrant for a property on South Street, and a court order on a property on the corner of Stony Lake and Clark Lake. Kirkpatrick will draft a document on what is allowed in reference to chickens and roosters. Assessing, Zoning, & Building: Written report for Building provided by Jane Gallant. Written report for Assessing provided by Lisa from All Level Assessing. Sewer & Water Operations: Wymer said leaks in the well casing of a township well were repaired at about a $15,000 cost. The lift station at the corner of Wolf Lake Road and Mack Island Road suffered a lightning strike that burned up the control panel, destroyed one of the pumps, and damaged another pump resulting in a 9,000-gallon sewage spill. The repair could take 30-45 days. This lift station is managed by Grass Lake Charter Township and they are researching whether they have insurance coverage on the lift station. Planning Commission: Hummer reported the commission did not meet in August and will not meet in September. Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA): Stage reported the ZBA met on August 12, 2026 for a variance request on Ackerson Lake Drive where steps were built down to the lake without permits. The request was denied. The steps have since been removed. The next meeting is September 9 for two cases. Page 1 of 3 September 8, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting NEW BUSINESS: Commuter Parking Area Designation: Wymer said a local resident contacted the township to use the township parking lot for University of Michigan commuters to park their personal cars. Wymer suggested created an area of 9 parking spaces for commuters to park near M-50. Stage asked about insurance coverage for the commuters. Wymer will contact the insurance company to make them aware and validate the township’s coverage. Motion by Wymer to designate 9 parking spaces for use as commuter parking spaces and to put in signage to designate those for public use, support by Stage. Roll Call: Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE. Motion carried. INegal Dumping in Road Right of Ways: Wymer shared an email from Jim Cole, senior project manager at Jackson County Department of Transportation regarding illegal dumping. Wymer said there have been complaints of dumping on Blue Ridge Road. Wymer asked the public for suggestions and their responses included: e Adding trail cams, More police patrols, Rewards to help catch violators, Contacting LRS Waste Management for assistance, and Posting no dumping signs. Wolf Lake Canal Weed Special Assessment District Motion by Wymer to approve the Resolution Initiating Process to Establish Wolf Lake Canal Special Assessment District, support by Graham. Roll Call: Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE. Motion carried. First public hearing will be held October 13 at SPM. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: Lakeview Avenue Road Special Assessment District — Resolution Continuing the Process First public hearing was held September 8 at SPM. There were no objections to the project or the parcels listed. Second public hearing is scheduled for Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 5:00PM. Motion by Wymer to approve the Resolution Continuing Process to Establish Lakeview Drive Special Assessment District for Road Improvements, support by Spring. Roll Call: Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE. Motion carried. Crypt Roof Replacement & Grant from Napoleon Benefit Fund Spring said Ryan Watts recently put out a request for donations to fill the $4,000 gap. So far, $500 has been collected. Page 2 of 3 September 8, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting Tire Collection Event Wymer recommended we select a date in October for the tire collection event for Grass Lake, Napoleon, and Norvell Township residents. The dates of October 17 and 24" were suggested as possibilities. Spring will check with the school to see what date works best for the students to help with the event. Motion by Wymer to authorize Clerk Spring to choose the date and secure volunteers for the tire collection event, support by Graham. Motion carried. UPDATES: 800 Mhz Radios Ballot Proposal: Leading up to the November election, Wymer said the 800 Mhz Radio committee is preparing information to be shared and individual municipalities are sharing information with residents. Part 41 Freeze — Thaw: During a recent meeting with EGLE, Wymer said EGLE agreed to lift the freeze for any townships connected to the Leoni Township Plant. EGLE will now consider approval of Part 41 permits for townships connected to the plant. JATA Support Letter: Wymer referenced a letter of support he provided to Jackson Area Transportation Authority ATA) for them to submit a grant for low or no-emission buses to replace aging vehicles. The letter was included in the board packet. Administrative Judge Unemployment Benefits Hearing: Wymer said a former employee filed a claim for unemployment benefits. While originally denied by the State of Michigan, it was appealed by the employee then approved by the State. The township objected to the approval so the claim is going through the process of a hearing with an administrative law judge. The first hearing meeting was on August 27; the next hearing is scheduled for September 17. Water Tower: Wymer said EGLE referred the township to a group called the Rural Community Assistance Partnership (RCAP) which helps local communities pursue grant money. Wymer has been in contact with the organization which provides services at no charge to the township. PUBLIC COMMENT - Any Township Business Cathy Rice of 8593 Glenwood Ct commented on the board’s approval of the commuter parking area designation. Nancy Kimball of 10079 Cady Rd shared information about a scrap metal drive on October 3 and 4 at the Napoleon Community School Bus Garage. Adjourn: 6:36 PM Traci Spring, Clerk Dan Wymer, Supervisor Page 3 of 3 September 8, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting Napoleon Township Special Board Meeting Lakeview Ave Special Assessment District Public Hearing 1 September 8, 2026 Call To Order 5:00 pm by Supervisor Wymer with members Graham, Hummer, Spring, and Stage present. Approximately 10 residents and property owners were present along with Jim Cole from the Jackson County Department of Transportation (SCDOT). Pledge of Allegiance Status Summary: Supervisor Wymer summarized the purpose of the meeting and the documents included. The first document listed all the parcel numbers and owner(s). Those highlighted in green signed the petition, four declined to sign, and four were unable to be reached. The approved signatures from the petition totaled 58.95% of the road frontage in the special assessment district. The second document included the price quote for the proposed work. Wymer explained the costs for the special assessment district will be allocated equally by lot and not figured by frontage. Randy Wagner of 7558 Lakeview resident asked how the long project would take and when it would start. Cole responded the project would take 1-2 weeks and start June or July 2027. Jim Cole from JCDOT explained the work to be done on the gravel road includes re-graveling at a thickness of 5” average with 23A gravel and a Perma Zyne substrate stabilizing application. Additionally, the first 50” will be paved from Rexford Road up to Lakeview Avenue. The county is using the substrate for this first time to see how it works on a neighborhood road. Many other counties use this method. Audrey Tierney of 7817 Lakeview Ave asked about what happens to existing cement driveways. Cole responded that the JCDOT will slope an approach to meet the driveways so there is no bump. James Sherzer of 7814 Lakeview Ave mentioned the amount of traffic due to garbage trucks, delivery trucks, etc. Cole said this is still considered residential traffic. Patric Tierney of 7817 Lakeview Ave asked about the life expectancy of a gravel road. Cole said it’s 12 years, but it’s likely been 25-30 years since these roads have been regraveled. The road will be regraveled to the correct width. Correcting any current drainage issues is not within the current scope of work. The road should not have to be brined due to the substrate. Tim Holland of 7663 Lakeview Ave asked about the lifespan of the proposed improvements. Cole responded it should last 10-12 years and no warranty is included on the work. Holland also asked about maintenance of the road after it’s improved and whether it will need to be regraded. Cole said the goal is not to grade it for a year or two. Linda Holland of 7663 Lakeview Ave asked if this would make the road smooth. Cole said it will still be a gravel road. Trustee Wagner stated that it is difficult to find Class 1 e-bikes to purchase. He believes most are Class 2. ADJOURNMENT ublic Participation P All regular and special meetings, hearings, records, and accounts shall be open to the public. Public comment shall be allowed at all meetings. 1. All public comment should be presented during the time(s) designated on the agenda. Public comment is normally not allowed outside of those times; however, sometimes the Commission may recognize members of the public to speak. 2. Public comment at all Commission meetings shall be conducted according to the following rules: a. The Chair opens the meeting for public comment and summarizes the rules of conduct for public comments as outlined in this section. For public hearings, the Chair will also announce the topic under consideration. b. All public speakers are encouraged to identify themselves by full name and community of residence prior to speaking. c. All comments must be addressed to the Chair. d. Speakers are given only three minutes each. Speakers are not permitted to grant their time to an alternate speaker. During public hearings, public comment and discussion shall be limited to the topic under consideration. Bylaws and Rules of Procedure Adopted May 5, 2026 Saline Township Planning Commission Page 10 of 12 e. Commission response to public comments shall be confined to clarification of the presented facts. f. Each person will be given an opportunity to be heard. After every person interested in addressing the Commission has spoken, the Chair may permit additional public comments. g. The Chair may limit the amount of time allowed for each person wishing to make public comment at a Commission meeting. The Chair may ask members of the audience to caucus with others sharing similar positions so they may select a single spokesperson. If a single spokesperson is selected, that individual shall be able to make public comment at the Commission meeting without time limit or an extended time limit. isorderly conduct at meetings D 1. Members of the public shall not interrupt Commission members, Liaisons, or individuals permitted to address the Commission while they are speaking during a meeting or otherwise disrupt a Commission meeting. 2. The Chair may call to order any attendee who: a. Engages in personal attacks which disrupt the meeting, incite violence or raise issues that are unrelated to Commission business; b. Uses obscene or grossly indecent language; c. Speaks longer than the allotted time; d. Disrupts the proceedings; e. Otherwise violates the rules of the Commission. 3. Failure to come to order may result in the forfeiture of any remaining speaking time, or, at the request of the Chair, expulsion from the meeting.

Chairperson Galley addressed the discussion that occurred before the previous meeting regarding the Pledge of Allegiance. He stated that he supports reciting the Pledge and explained that when he served on the Planning Commission in Independence Township, the Pledge was recited at every meeting. He said that when he came to Springfield Township, he found it unusual that the Pledge was not recited and had previously asked about it but did not receive a resolution. He stated that he understood the practice was a carryover from the previous administration and that Springfield Township now has a township-wide practice of reciting the Pledge at every meeting. Commissioner Ruth Ann Hines stated that she had served on the Planning Commission for many years and that the Planning Commission had never traditionally started meetings with the Pledge. Chairperson Galley clarified that the previous practice was not intentional and confirmed that the Planning Commission would proceed with the Pledge of Allegiance at its meetings. Commissioners In Attendance: Brian Galley, Chair Andrew Donato Ruth Ann Hines Steve Felix Kevin Sclesky Commissioners Absent: Consultants’ Present: Megan Masson-Minock, Township Planner Jason Mayer, Township Engineer Approval of Agenda: Commissioner Felix moved to approve the consent agenda as written. Commissioner Hines supported. Vote. Yes: Galley, Hines, Sclesky, Felix. No: None. Absent: None. Motion approved. Approval of Consent Agenda: 1) Approve Minutes of August 25, 2026 Regular Meeting 1 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 Commissioner Hines moved to approve the consent agenda with the correction on page 2, a motion she made to approve the consent agenda was recorded as a motion to approve the agenda. She requested that the word “consent” be added for clarification. Commissioner Felix supported. Vote. Yes: Galley, Hines, Sclesky, Felix. No: None. Absent: None. Motion approved. Public Hearing: 1) Rezoning Request – 10774 Dixie Hwy – 07-03-126-001 Planner Megan Masson-Minock provided an overview of the application located at 10774 Dixie Highway. She explained that the property owner and applicant proposed rezoning approximately 3.98 acres of an existing 20-plus-acre parcel located on the east side of Dixie Highway, southeast of the intersection of Dixie Highway and Oak Hill Road. She explained that the parcel has an unusual configuration and that the applicant proposed rezoning the approximately four-acre portion along Dixie Highway from R-1 to Local Business District, C-1. A formal lot split application was submitted at the same time. Planner Masson-Minock stated that, after discussing the proposal with Brian Piper from Assessing, the proposed lot split could be approved administratively as a flag lot. She explained that while split zoning on one parcel can sometimes be a concern, the applicant intended to separate the commercial portion from the remaining residential property. The remaining property would remain zoned R-1 and the applicant had also submitted a proposal for a single-family home. Planner Masson-Minock stated that the proposal was consistent with the Township Master Plan, which identifies the Dixie Highway frontage in this area for commercial use and the rear portion for low-density, single-family residential use. She explained that a rezoning review requires consideration of all permitted and special land uses within the proposed zoning district. Examples of permitted C-1 uses include office buildings, training or educational centers, personal service establishments, data processing or computer centers, retail businesses such as grocery stores, bakeries, clothing and shoe stores, and fitness facilities. Planner Masson-Minock explained that Special land uses that would require public hearing and 300-foot notification include automobile repair facilities, gas stations, daycare centers, automobile washes, shortterm rentals, and bed and breakfast establishments. She also discussed potential traffic impacts. She estimated that approximately two single-family homes could generate approximately 19 trips per day, while a variety store could generate more than 1,000 trips per day, a small office building could generate nearly 400 trips per day, and a convenience store or gas station could generate approximately 265 trips per day. She stated that the area was planned for commercial development and that Dixie Highway is a large roadway that would likely have the capacity to accommodate additional traffic. She also noted that the findings of fact were included on page 7 of the review letter and could be discussed following the public hearing. 2 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 Chair Galley opened the public hearing at 7:08 p.m. and invited members of the public to speak regarding the proposed rezoning. Ms. Stephanie Nahas stated that he was concerned with Planner’s Masson-Minock’s comment that Dixie Highway was a large road capable of handling the additional traffic. She stated that this may not be the case if the Road Commission proceeds with its proposal to narrow the roadway. He said that the road would become more condensed and could potentially result in more accidents. She stated that she did not believe the statement regarding the roadway’s capacity was accurate and suggested that it be reconsidered. Mr. Landis stated that he represented a very old family, the Landins, whose family had owned property in the area for nearly 190 years. He explained that when his grandfather sold the property behind their homes, it was stated to the Board at that time that the property would never become commercial. If the property were to become commercial against their wishes, he requested that the property owner be required to install a berm, wall, fence, or other protective measure for the homes that had been there for approximately 189 years. Mr. Landis stated that he had lived on the property for nearly 60 years and was the fifth generation to live there, along with his younger brother. He said that his family valued the peace and quiet behind their home and did not believe commercial development would be a good idea. Mr. Landis stated that when the residential property was developed along Dixie Highway and Rattalee Lake Road, the additional noise was enough to keep his family awake early in the morning. He said that the area was currently quiet and that the residents of the nearby homes did not cause interference, but businesses could create additional noise and trash. He stated that he did not want that behind his home and intended to remain in his house for the rest of his life. He also mentioned the bar located near the front of the property and stated that the noise could already be heard when the doors were open. He expressed concern about the possibility of additional noise from gas stations or other businesses, particularly businesses that might operate 24 hours a day. He stated that Oak Hill Road had been quiet his entire life but had become busier and noisier after it was paved. He said he now hears teenagers driving up and down the road in modified vehicles and did not want additional traffic and noise behind his home late at night. Mr. Landis reiterated that he opposed creating a commercial zone, particularly because his grandfather had stated at the time of the sale that the property behind their home was to remain residential and the Board at the time had agreed. Another member of the public suggested that the Township include a map when posting rezoning notices so residents could clearly see which parcels were being discussed. The speaker stated that this would be helpful for all rezoning cases and would make it easier for residents to understand the locations being considered rather than only seeing an address. Chair Galley agreed that a larger visual map could be helpful. 3 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 There being no further speakers, Chair Galley closed the public hearing regarding 10774 Dixie Highway at 7:15 p.m. Old Business: 1) Data Center Ordinance Amendments Review The first item under Old Business is the draft data center zoning ordinance amendments. Planner MassonMinock explained that at the previous Planning Commission meeting, the Commission reviewed the draft zoning ordinance amendments and decided to form a subcommittee to review the amendments. The subcommittee consists of Chairperson Galley, Trustee/Planning Commissioner Sclesky, Planning Commissioner Donato, and Township resident Brandon Boucher, an energy engineer with the University of Michigan. The subcommittee met on September 10, 2026, at Township Hall and provided directions and edits to Carlisle Wortman. Planner Masson-Minock stated that the draft ordinance was currently being revised based on the subcommittee’s input. Once revised, it would be circulated to the Fire Department, Township Engineer, and Township Attorney for review. The goal was to circulate the draft by the end of the week so comments could be received and incorporated before the Planning Commission’s October meeting. She stated that the revised draft would need to be ready at least one week before the October meeting to be included in the meeting packet. Commissioner Sclesky asked whether the subcommittee would meet again after a clean copy was prepared to review the entire document. Planner Masson-Minock confirmed that it would. Chairperson Galley stated that Brandon Boucher’s experience as an energy engineer with the University of Michigan was very valuable to the subcommittee. He explained that Mr. Boucher reviewed the existing ordinance line by line and provided guidance regarding what was realistic, what could be strengthened, and what could be made more or less restrictive. He stated that having an experienced resident participate in the process was very helpful and appreciated the additional expertise. Commissioner Sclesky also recognized Planning Commissioner Donato for his experience and knowledge regarding data centers. He stated that the discussion between Commissioner Donato and Mr. Boucher was very helpful and that the subcommittee was able to combine their technical knowledge with the practical perspectives of the Township representatives. He stated that the existing ordinance was reviewed in detail and that portions of the language were simplified and improved. He said he looked forward to reviewing the clean copy and completing the final revisions. 4 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 Commissioner Donato stated that he believed the Township was developing strong and well-thought-out standards based on examples from other communities, including Pittsfield. He said the Township had the opportunity to learn from the experiences of other communities and establish regulations that would provide long-term protection for the Township. Commissioner Sclesky stated that he considered the subcommittee’s work one of the most valuable uses of committee time in a long time. He said the process had been very informative and that he was glad to have been involved, particularly because the subcommittee was able to receive resident input and use a high level of experience and knowledge in developing the ordinance. Chairperson Galley stated that once the revised draft was completed, it would be emailed to the individuals involved for another review and meeting. He said the Township should then be able to place a draft on the Township website for the public to review. He stated that the goal was to have a strong final draft ready for the Planning Commission’s next meeting. New Business: 1. 10774 Dixie Hwy Rezoning Application – 07-03-126-001 The first item in New Business is the 10774 Dixie Highway rezoning application, Parcel ID No. 07-03-126001. The applicant, Adam Magaluk, addressed the Commission. Mr. Magaluk stated that Planner MassonMinock had accurately summarized his intentions. He explained that he recently purchased approximately 21-acre property in June and was looking for a recreational area for his family. He stated that he lives in Birmingham and grew up in Milford, where he had a large backyard, and was looking for a place outside of the city where his family could ride four-wheelers and enjoy recreational activities. He also stated that he enjoys paintball and intended to use the wooded portion of the property as a personal recreational area. He had submitted permits for a single-family home. Mr. Magaluk explained that the approximately three to four acres along Dixie Highway, with approximately 425 feet of frontage, appeared to him to be a good location for commercial development. He stated that he did not personally need that portion for his recreational use and did not believe it was an ideal location for a house or recreational area. His intent was therefore to split the parcel and rezone the Dixie Highway frontage for commercial use while keeping the remaining acreage residential. Chairperson Galley asked where Mr. Magaluk intended to place the home. Mr. Magaluk stated that the home would be located approximately in the middle of the property and would be within the required setbacks. He stated that the building permit application showed the proposed location. 5 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 Chairperson Galley asked whether the wooded portion of the property would remain primarily wooded. Mr. Magaluk stated that he intended to keep as much of the woods as possible, with trails for recreational use, along with the home and a paintball field. Chairperson Galley asked whether Mr. Magaluk was a commercial developer and whether he intended to sell the commercial portion in the future. Mr. Magaluk stated that he was not a commercial developer and worked in technology, but that he would likely list the commercial property for sale or work with a broker to sell or develop it. Any future purchaser would still have to go through the Township’s review process. Chairperson Galley asked Planner Masson-Minock whether any future commercial development would have to comply with the Township’s zoning requirements. Planner Masson-Minock confirmed that all zoning ordinance requirements would be enforced during site plan review. She explained that any new non-residential building would require site plan review and that buffering requirements between commercial and residential uses would apply. These requirements could include landscaping and, in some circumstances, a wall. Planner Masson-Minock explained that the Planning Commission’s action that evening was to make a recommendation to the Township Board. Because the request involved an ordinance and a zoning map amendment, the Township Board would need to conduct two readings. She reviewed the six findings of fact from September 14, 2026, in her letter. The proposed rezoning would change approximately 3.9 acres from R-1, One Family Residential, to C-1, Local Business, as part of an existing 20-plus-acre parcel. The proposed lot lines matched the proposed rezoning boundaries. The lot split would be reviewed by Township Zoning and Assessing staff after the rezoning decision, and staff had indicated that the proposed lot split could be approved if the rezoning occurred. Planner Masson-Minock stated that the proposed rezoning was consistent with elements of the Township Master Plan. The subject property was planned for local commercial use and was located within the North Dixie Highway Overlay District, which was established to accommodate a mix of uses. She stated that the proposed C-1 zoning designation appeared to support that intent and would also support the Master Plan objective of providing commercial and service uses that meet the convenience needs of residents while serving as a transition between lower and higher intensity land uses. Planner Masson-Minock stated that the area proposed for rezoning was primarily vacant, with some portions of existing gravel driveways, and appeared to have few, if any, natural features. The rezoning would allow more intensive use than those currently permitted under R-1. If rezoned, the property owner could pursue any permitted or special land use allowed in the C-1 district, subject to applicable zoning 6 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING September 22, 2026 requirements. She also stated that the proposed commercial area met the minimum lot requirements for the C-1 district and that the remaining parcel would meet the requirements of Section 40-642, which would allow a reduction in lot width to permit the proposed lot split under the R-1 zoning. She explained that the resulting configuration would be a flag lot. Planner Masson-Minock also discussed traffic. She stated that a C-1 rezoning had the potential to increase the number of vehicle trips per day compared to the existing R-1 zoning. However, the property was located on Dixie Highway, which was planned for a variety of land uses, including uses that could generate higher traffic volumes. She noted that the Township’s Master Plan had been adopted approximately two years earlier and that the current discussion by the Road Commission regarding a potential road diet or reduction in the width of Dixie Highway had not been contemplated when the Master Plan was adopted. She stated that this could be considered a changed circumstance. Commissioner Sclesky discussed the Road Commission’s proposal for Dixie Highway and stated that the proposal had not been well received by the communities along the roadway. He noted that a joint meeting of the Planning Commission and Township Board was planned and suggested that the supervisors from the other affected communities participate so that the communities could discuss a united response and possible alternatives. He stated that he would prefer to find a way to create a center turn lane without reducing the roadway to one lane and suggested that improvements could be made gradually over time. Variance Application ZBA 26-001 requesting approval to demolish the two existing single-family homes located at 1484 and 1488 Ridge Road, combine the two parcels into one lot and construct a new 2,606 square foot single-family home with an attached 600 square foot garage. Korf, applicant, explained the rationale for the current site plan and requested the speciﬁc concerns of the ZBA members since the site plan projected setbacks were improved from the existing situation. Chairperson Kiss led the discussion related to the following issues: • Although the projected setbacks are an improvement to the existing buildings on the lots, the proposed home design exceeds the established 30% Floor Area Ratio (FAR) limits. Blissick stated that the FAR limit was 20% originally but was increased to 30% as a more reasonable limit for current single-family homes in the area. Pacheco commented the current site plan cannot be approved at tonight’s meeting due to inaccuracies in the calculated FAR and square footage of the home as presented; however, the applicant may re-apply with an updated site plan. There is a mandatory re-notiﬁcation process required due to an inaccurate public notice and the township will follow its standard operating procedures for handling project submittals and fees. • Kiss noted the consensus of the members that the site plan must have a maximum FAR of 30% (currently 44% in the application). Pacheco noted the basement is not part of the FAR. • Kiss expressed concern that the basement of the home must be 50% or greater under the natural grade of the property. No ﬁll dirt can be used to get to 50%. Blissick reiterated the need to have 50% or more of the basement be underground the natural grade of the property. • Kiss indicated a requirement of the measurements of the four outer walls including the 2nd ﬂoor. • Kiss said it appears one porch is enclosed? Korf responded there is no enclosure and neither is the porch screened. • Kiss asked that the HVAC unit be moved to the road side of the house to minimize the noise to the neighbors. • Bareis noted the building will be close to the existing lot lines. • Kiss and Blissick expressed they had no issues with the proposed setbacks. They are an improvement from the existing situation. • Kiss noted the home should be approximately 2,600 square feet. • Kiss asked the applicant whether they would prefer their application be denied or tabled at tonight’s meeting. Applicant preferred tabling. 4 Sylvan Township Zoning Board of Appeals Meeting July 22, 2026 Page 3 of 3 Moved by Kiss, supported by Bareis to table consideration of Variance Application ZBA 26-001 to allow for the necessary design revisions and re-notiﬁcation for a public hearing and consideration at a future meeting.
